items.title: Borno community to Tinubu, Zulum: Bring our 78 children home
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike & Kehinde Folarin ABUJA – The Margi community in Borno State has urged President Bola Tinubu and Governor Babagana Zulum to intensify efforts to rescue 78 schoolchildren and a teacher abducted from Mussa and Lassa communities in Askira/Uba Local Government Area. The community said the victims’ continued captivity had plunged their families into anguish, urging the authorities to step up rescue efforts and provide regular updates on their whereabouts. Briefing journalists in Abuja on Thursday, the community’s Secretary, Malla Gadzama, said 43 pupils were abducted from Mussa on May 15, 2026, while 35 students and a teacher were taken from a secondary school in Lassa on June 26 as they prepared for national examinations. “Our message is simple and clear: our children must not be forgotten,” Gadzama said. He called on Tinubu to mobilise the necessary security and intelligence resources and ensure effective coordination among security agencies. “Mr President, these children are Nigerians. Their lives matter,” he added. Gadzama also urged Zulum to make the rescue a priority and establish a reliable channel for keeping affected families informed without compromising security operations. “Development must also be measured by the safety of our children and the well-being of their families. Infrastructure cannot compensate for the continuing anguish of parents whose children remain in captivity,” he said. The community appealed to Senator Ali Ndume and other elected representatives from Askira/Uba to use their positions to sustain pressure on the authorities. It also called for better security around vulnerable schools and medical, psychological and educational support for the victims upon their return. Citing Section 14(2)(b) of the 1999 Constitution, which identifies the security and welfare of the people as the primary purpose of government, Gadzama said the authorities must fulfil their constitutional responsibility. “We are not asking for favour from government. We are just asking the government to fulfil its primary responsibility to the people,” he said. The community urged Tinubu, Zulum and security agencies to sustain rescue efforts until the children and their teacher were safely reunited with their families. “Bring Mussa schoolchildren, Lassa schoolchildren and their teachers safely home. That is our demand,” Gadzama said. The post Borno community to Tinubu, Zulum: Bring our 78 children home appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Cantines scolaires en Guinée : 20 milliards GNF et des stocks inexpliqués au cœur d’une enquête de la CRIEF
items.description: Le parquet spécial près la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (CRIEF) a ordonné l’ouverture d’une enquête sur la gestion des fonds alloués à la Direction nationale des cantines scolaires (DNCaS). Une enveloppe de 20 milliards de francs guinéens, des stocks de vivres dont la consommation ne serait pas justifiée et des soupçons d’irrégularités dans l’attribution des marchés publics figurent parmi les faits signalés. Dans une instruction adressée au directeur central de l’ORDEF le procureur spécial près la CRIEF demande l’ouverture d’une enquête préliminaire pour des faits présumés de détournement de deniers publics et de corruption. Selon le document, le signalement transmis au parquet fait état d’irrégularités dans l’utilisation des subventions publiques destinées à l’approvisionnement des établissements scolaires en vivres. Les investigations devront notamment porter sur une enveloppe de 20 milliards de francs guinéens allouée en 2021, ainsi que sur 200 millions de francs guinéens destinés au suivi des activités. L’utilisation de ces ressources n’aurait fait l’objet d’aucune justification comptable et financière, d’après les éléments rapportés au parquet. Au-delà des fonds engagés, la gestion des stocks alimentaires suscite également des interrogations. Pour l’exercice 2025-2026, d’importantes quantités de riz, d’huile, de haricots et de sel auraient été acquises pour répondre aux besoins de 58 691 élèves répartis dans 450 établissements scolaires. Mais les stocks livrés en mai 2026, censés couvrir 83 jours de classe, étaient déjà en voie d’épuisement en octobre, selon le signalement. Aucun rapport de synthèse ne permettrait de justifier la consommation de ces denrées. Le document mentionne également des écarts entre les effectifs d’élèves déclarés et ceux qui bénéficieraient réellement du programme. Le signalement transmis au parquet évoque par ailleurs de possibles irrégularités dans la passation des marchés publics. Certains contrats auraient été attribués à des groupements liés à la direction chargée de la gestion des cantines scolaires. Autre fait rapporté : des bons de livraison auraient été transmis aux services déconcentrés pour recueillir des signatures préalables au paiement, sans livraison effective des denrées correspondantes. Ces allégations devront être vérifiées au cours de l’enquête afin d’établir les circonstances des faits et les éventuelles responsabilités individuelles. Dans son instruction, le procureur spécial demande à l’ORDEF de procéder sans délai à l’interpellation et à l’audition de Saran Fadima Kaba et de Mariame Camara. Toute autre personne dont la responsabilité pénale personnelle serait établie devra également être entendue. Les investigations seront conduites sous la direction de trois substituts du procureur spécial près la CRIEF : Ousmane Sanoh, Pierre Segbé Kamano et Biwon Millimono. Créée en 2015, la Direction nationale des cantines scolaires est chargée de contribuer à l’approvisionnement des établissements scolaires en vivres. L’enquête devra remonter à cette date pour examiner la gestion financière, comptable et matérielle des ressources mises à sa disposition jusqu’à aujourd’hui.

items.title: Ghanaian neuroscientist honoured at Millennium Excellence Awards USA for Alzheimer’s blood test discovery
items.description: Thomas Karikari, associate professor of psychiatry and clinical and translational science at the University of Pittsburgh’s School of Medicine in the United States, was a proud recipient of the Excellence in Scientific Research award at the recent Millennium Excellence Awards ceremony in Washington, DC, under the royal patronage of Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the Asantehene. When young Dr. Thomas Karikari entered his laboratory in Sweden years ago for his research program, one question lingered on his mind: “Why don’t we have a good blood test kit for Alzheimer’s dementia?” This was a question that not only developed into a hypothesis for research, but one that was ready to transform biomedical research in neuroscience and enhance medical care for people living with the condition. Many scientists had attempted in their might to understand how the disease could be easily tested without an invasive procedure, but failed at it. Dr. Karikari was nearly discouraged in his quest for answers. “I was told you don’t talk about it. Companies have spent millions; they couldn’t do it. People have spent years, but they couldn’t do it. So, just shut up,” he recounted. But, burning with the desire, the neuroscientist was poised to develop his question into a groundbreaking practical solution to testing the neurological disorder with blood samples. ‘And I set out to do it as my side project. I wasn’t even doing it as my main project because no one believed it would work,” he noted. For decades, diagnosing Alzheimer’s required invasive procedures such as spinal taps or expensive brain scans. These tests are often inaccessible in many regions of the world, especially in low-resource communities. Dr. Karikari’s experience with limited diagnostic capacity in Ghana fueled the need for a solution. So, when he was headhunted to lead a clinical research program in diagnostic medicine at the University of Pittsburgh in the United States of America (USA), he was bent on dedicating most of his career to developing, improving, and validating the clinical performance of blood tests that could simplify Alzheimer’s diagnosis. After grueling years and sleepless nights at the lab, he finally found a means to detect the disease. Dr. Karikari has about 300 publications to his name. He has published multiple seminal works in leading medical journals describing major innovations in high-performance blood tests for the neurological disorder. He also holds several patents and pending patents to that effect. Last year, Dr. Karikari was recognized by Clarivate as among the top 1% of scientists worldwide. The high-impact journal Nature also named him as a Rising Star in Ageing research, an accolade that was bestowed on only three investigators. These accomplishments have earned Dr. Karikari global respect and recognition as a leading figure in biomedical research. His achievements were celebrated at the just-ended Millennium Excellence Awards USA, spearheaded by the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II. “I am so proud that today I have made that contribution. A contribution that would change the face of how we treat diseases for a long time. This is just a stepping stone,” he gladly noted. Dr. Thomas Karikari’s groundbreaking research has led to the development of multiple blood tests for Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia. In his acceptance speech, Dr. Karikari further noted that two new blood tests for Alzheimer’s disease have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This adds to two already approved by the authority over the last two years. Dr. Karikari’s mission is beyond scientific discovery—he wants diagnostics to reach everyone, including people in places like his home village of Manfo. He says a parcel of land has been acquired back home in his late mother’s hometown of Achinakrom near Ejisu in the Ashanti region to continue with the groundbreaking scientific discoveries in Ghana. He is poised to establish a research center to help advance biomedical research on the continent. “Everything we do must get back to our people,” he said.

items.title: L’oeil de Guinéenews : un taxi en surcharge excessive s’immobilise en pleine chaussée
items.description: La scène que l'on voit là, quoique assez fréquente chez nous, ne va pas manquer pas de faire réagir les usagers de la route, surtout dans la capitale. Un taxi de transport en commun, visiblement trop lourdement chargé, a rendu l'âme en plein milieu de la voie. Il a le capot grand ouvert et crée, en même temps, un véritable calvaire pour les automobilistes et les motocyclistes. Immobilisé dans une zone stratégique et particulièrement exigüe, précisément sous un pont, le véhicule en panne, a aussitôt, bloqué le flux de la circulation. Entre les klaxons impatients et rageurs, les cris et récriminations venant de tous les côtés, c'est un tumulte sans fin. Le chauffeur et le convoyeur ne savent plus où donner de la tête. Ils sont partagés entre plusieurs sentiments : le trauma qu'ils subissent du fait des cris sans limite et sans fin, l'impatience qu'ils ont de livrer les bagages à temps et le souci pour leur sécurité et aussi, pour le dépannage du véhicule. Pendant ce temps, les usagers alentour sont piégés dans les embouteillages. C'est l'une des facettes de notre circulation routière. Un environnement encombré, désorganisé, peut être même anarchique, sous certans aspects. Ce qui crée le stress chez tout le monde et contribue à rendre la circulation, difficile à se dérouler correctement. En effet, elle est loin d'être apaisée. D'où les embouteillages et accidents fréquents. A cela, s'ajoutent, deux autres aspects, non des moindres: c'est d'abord la question du respect des normes de chargement et de l’état technique des véhicules de transport public sur les axes routiers de notre pays. Deux exigences qui attendent toujours d'être effectives pour tout le monde, dans notre pays. La même remarque s'applique au conducteur de deux roues que l'on voit ici, sur l'image. Il est casqué et porte des chaussures fermées, ce qui est déjà appréciable en soi. Mais, il a deux passagers au lieu de un seul, comme le prescrit la règlementation en vigueur. De cela, nous parlerons dans les jours à venir.

items.title: ‘No country developed in less than 30 years’, Kashifu defends Tinubu
items.description: .As TMS unveils new platform By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Director General of the National Information Technology Development Agency NITDA, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, has defended the reforms of President Bola Tinubu, saying no country has developed in less than 30 years. Kashifu, who is also Chairman, Board of Trustees and National Coordinator of the Tinubu Movement for Sustainable Governance Foundation (TMS), spoke on Thursday in Abuja at the group’s inaugural training workshop. “No country in the world developed in less than 30 years. The fastest developed country is South Korea. It took 30 years. To develop, you need the right policies first. That is the foundation Mr President is laying. Then you build on it to get investors,” he said. The programme, themed ‘Empowering Every Nigerian to be Heard’, also saw the Movement launch its official website, http://tmsnigeria.ng, where citizens can engage and verify information. The event was convened to educate citizens on the Renewed Hope Agenda and to give Nigerians a platform to contribute ideas on how to move the country forward. Kashifu said the thrust of the reforms is a change in what government spends its money on. “We spend most of our resources trying to subsidise consumption. When President Bola Ahmed Tinubu came on board, he looked at it: Is it consumption we should subsidise, or production, innovation, and investment? That is what the reforms are all about,” he said. According to him, the President built the Renewed Hope Agenda around eight priority areas. They are reforming the economy for sustained growth; strengthening national security; boosting agriculture for food security; unlocking energy and natural resources; enhancing infrastructure and transportation; focusing on health, education and social investment; accelerating diversification through industrialisation, digitalisation and creative industry; and improving governance through efficient service delivery. The NITDA chief pointed to the integration of digital skills into formal education, the introduction of Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) by the Ministry of Education, and the Student Loan scheme, which he said ensures no Nigerian is left behind because of economic circumstances. He added that NITDA is promoting digital literacy through Digital Literacy for All, the training of over 19,000 National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) champions in markets and motor parks, and the Three Million Tech Talent programme, which prepares young Nigerians to work remotely for global companies. Kashifu said the reforms are already attracting investors, citing the Dangote Refinery, a $1 billion data centre investment by a South African firm announced this week, and JP Morgan’s decision to open operations in Nigeria. “Reform is a journey; it is not a one-off event. The essence of this movement is to enlighten Nigerians on these reforms, so that Nigerians can understand what is in it for them. You are the ultimate beneficiary,” he said. He urged participants at the roundtable to propose ideas on how to sustain the reforms and to state what government needs to do more, including inputs for the approved National Youth Conference. A member of the TMS Board of Trustees, Olujonwo Obasanjo, said the Movement was set up to close the information gap between government and citizens and to showcase progress being recorded through projects across the country. He described the creation of regional development commissions by President Tinubu, and his commitment to local government autonomy affirmed by the Supreme Court, as deliberate steps to fast-track inclusive development and bring governance closer to the people. “Nigeria’s development challenge has never been lack of ideas, but policy discontinuity. There is the need for sustained, uninterrupted reforms to consolidate gains, drive economic growth and ensure that ongoing investments translate into lasting prosperity,” Obasanjo stated. The Director-General of TMS, Marcel Ngogbehei, said the workshop was conceived to empower and educate ordinary Nigerians and give them a credible platform to be heard on national issues. He explained that the training combined civic education with practical engagement, including role-play sessions in which participants set public expectations of governance against what the Tinubu administration is already implementing. Ngogbehei acknowledged that reforms come with initial pains, but maintained that continuity is critical to attracting long-term investment and ensuring the benefits eventually reach every household. He urged Nigerians to move beyond rhetoric and demand substance from political actors. “Instead of following rhetoric, we should encourage Nigerians to ask the opposition a simple question: What alternative are you offering that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is not already doing?” he said. The post ‘No country developed in less than 30 years’, Kashifu defends Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama appoints 15 officers of the Ghana Prisons Service
items.description: President John Mahama has appointed 15 officers of the Ghana Prisons Service, elevating seven Deputy Directors of Prisons to Directors of Prisons and eight Assistant Directors of Prisons to Deputy Directors of Prisons. In a statement issued on Thursday, October 29, it said the appointments, which took effect on July 1, 2026, were made in accordance with Article 207 of the 1992 Constitution, on the advice of the Prisons Service Council. The seven officers appointed to the rank of Director of Prisons are Abraham Nii Moi Allotey, David Ofosu Addo, Thompson Otsyokpo, Edward Ashun, Joseph Asabre, Alfred Moses Cudjoe and Samuel Fiifi Dontoh. Mr Allotey is the Western Regional Commander and Officer-in-Charge of Sekondi Central Prison, while Mr Ofosu Addo serves as Head of Government Business at Prisons Headquarters. Mr Otsyokpo is the Bono-Ahafo Regional Commander and Officer-in-Charge of Sunyani Central Prison. Mr Ashun serves as Greater Accra Regional Commander and Commanding Officer at Prisons Headquarters, while Mr Asabre is the Central Regional Commander and Officer-in-Charge of Ankaful Maximum Security Prison. Mr Cudjoe serves as General Staff Officer at Prisons Headquarters, while Mr Dontoh is Head of Procurement at the headquarters. The eight officers appointed from Assistant Directors of Prisons to Deputy Directors of Prisons are Joseph Aggrey-Graham, Gandaa Bekanuo Zunuo, Aaron Agbenyegah Agbo, Michael Osei Akoto, Forson Odei, Naja Daniel Donkor, Nasom Kwabena Bawah and Matilda Nyampong. The Ghana Prisons Service congratulated the officers and wished them success as they take on their new responsibilities. The Service reaffirmed its commitment to professionalism, discipline and effective leadership, as well as its mandate of ensuring the safe custody, welfare, reformation and rehabilitation of prisoners.

items.title: 2027: Tinubu’s daughter mobilises market women, launches Iyaloja movement
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu’s daughter and Iyaloja-General of Nigeria, Dr Mujidat Folasade Tinubu-Ojo, has launched the Iyaloja General Movement (IGM) to mobilise market women and other grassroots voters for her father’s re-election in 2027. The movement, inaugurated on Thursday at Eagle Square, Abuja, comprises mainly market women from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with structures reportedly established across the country’s 774 local government areas and various electoral wards. The group pledged to mobilise 10 million votes for Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2027 general election. Speaking at the inauguration, Tinubu-Ojo said the movement would sensitise market leaders, traders and members of the informal sector about the forthcoming elections and encourage them to support candidates they consider capable of providing effective leadership. She said the group had coordinators and other officials at the state, local government and ward levels to drive its mobilisation efforts. According to her, market women and other informal-sector operators constitute an important voting bloc because of their presence in communities across the country. “What we are putting together as market leaders is to encourage our people and sensitise them on the next election — on which direction they should follow — so that they will not derail. And to inaugurate my own movement, the Iyaloja General Movement,” she said. Tinubu-Ojo urged voters to consider the direction of the country under the current administration, warning against electing candidates whose policies, in her view, could reverse the gains she attributed to the Tinubu administration. She expressed support for the President’s economic policies, acknowledging that they had imposed hardships on Nigerians but arguing that the expected long-term benefits justified the difficulties. “President Tinubu has done well. He has policies that will enhance the country and make our country boom again. We know what he has been doing,” she said. “What he is doing right now is like a pregnant woman going through labour. We are labouring now. Almost all Nigerians are feeling what he is doing now. The policies are painful, but the end result will justify the means.” The Iyaloja-General also defended the removal of the petrol subsidy, saying the additional revenue available to the three tiers of government had helped them execute projects and meet financial obligations, including the payment of workers’ salaries. She urged voters not to support a candidate who had promised to restore the subsidy, arguing that the revenue generated following its removal had enabled governments to undertake infrastructure projects. “We don’t want any person who will drive us back. If we vote somebody else now, that person will come with his own ideas. Somebody has said he is going to return the fuel subsidy, and we can see the impact of the fuel subsidy removal in the states,” she said. “We can see what the three tiers of government are doing. Workers are getting their salaries paid on time, and infrastructure is in place.” Tinubu-Ojo said the movement would work to sustain support for the President by engaging market associations and grassroots communities ahead of the election. items.description: Le gouverneur par intérim de la région administrative de Siguiri, le colonel Fadjimba Mara, a annoncé, ce jeudi 29 octobre 2026, la suspension de toutes les activités d’exploitation artisanale de l’or jusqu’à la régularisation de la situation. Selon le communiqué n°212/MATD/RAS/PS/2026, cette mesure vise à lutter contre la dégradation de l’environnement, la destruction des écosystèmes et la pollution des cours d’eau. Elle entend également préserver la sécurité des populations et garantir la quiétude sociale dans les zones concernées. Les autorités régionales pointent notamment du doigt l’utilisation de machines susceptibles d’entraîner d’importants dégâts environnementaux dans plusieurs localités aurifères de la région. Pour assurer l’application effective de cette décision, les préfets, les sous-préfets, les présidents de district ainsi que les responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité sont chargés de veiller au respect de la mesure sur le terrain. Le gouverneur par intérim invite enfin les populations à faire preuve de compréhension et de responsabilité face à cette décision, présentée comme une mesure de protection de l’environnement et de préservation de la sécurité publique.

items.title: ICPC arraigns PFIPC’s Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts
items.description: The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) on Thursday arraigned Adeniyi Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts of alleged forgery, impersonation and related offences before an FCT High Court in Abuja over his purported role as director-general of the Presidential Foreign Investment Promotion Council (PFIPC). Adeyemi pleaded not guilty to all the counts. The fresh arraignment followed the striking out of an earlier eight-count charge against him by a Federal High Court in Abuja on October 12, after the Federal Government sought to terminate the proceedings following a review by the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF). Rotimi Oyedepo, Director of Public Prosecutions of the Federation, had told the court that the review established that the alleged offences fell within the jurisdiction of the FCT High Court rather than the Federal High Court, where the police initially filed the charge. The prosecution subsequently filed the fresh charge before the FCT High Court. Forgery, impersonation allegations In the new charge, the ICPC accused Adeyemi of forging a letter dated March 8, 2024, purportedly signed by Femi Gbajabiamila, Chief of Staff to the President, appointing him director-general of the PFIPC. The commission alleged that Adeyemi used forged documents to present the purported council as a legitimate government institution and gain access to government facilities and official processes. Other counts accuse him of forging an executive order purportedly establishing the council and a legislative instrument bearing the titles of the Presidential Economic Advisory Council and PFIPC. The ICPC also alleged that he forged a document addressed to the Accountant-General of the Federation seeking approval for the purported agency to operate within the government’s financial reporting structure. Another allegation concerns documents purportedly submitted to the National Information Technology Development Agency to obtain a domain name for the council. The commission further accused Adeyemi of using forged documents presented to the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy to seek more than N27 billion for the establishment of the purported agency and N3.8 billion for personnel costs. In separate counts, the ICPC alleged that Adeyemi gave N210,000 to Aminu Abdullahi, an assistant chief technical officer in the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, to facilitate the allocation of office space without official authorisation. He was also accused of giving N300,000 to Ogaba Harry, an officer in the Office of the Chief Economic Adviser to the President, to facilitate the release of a Prado sport utility vehicle and a Land Cruiser. The commission further alleged that Adeyemi obtained N20 million from Oyekunle Gbenga, managing director of Divine Dopacy Nigeria Limited, under the pretence of a project facilitation loan for a purported N2.8 billion contract to furnish and renovate the official residence of the PFIPC director-general. The alleged offences reportedly occurred between 2024 and 2026 and are punishable under relevant provisions of the Penal Code, the Advance Fee Fraud and Other Fraud Related Offences Act, and the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act. Adeyemi has denied the allegations. He has separately alleged that Gbajabiamila collected N400 million through a proxy in connection with the appointment letter. The allegation against Gbajabiamila remains a claim by Adeyemi and is not established by the charges outlined in court. Court orders written bail application After Adeyemi entered his plea, ICPC counsel, Fatima Bardi, asked the court to fix a date for the commencement of trial. Defence counsel, Ibrahim Angulu, made an oral application for bail, but the presiding judge, Halilu Yusuf, directed him to file a formal written application. Angulu agreed but urged the court to schedule an early hearing, citing his client’s prolonged detention and health concerns. He told the court that Adeyemi had spent 155 days in detention and had a medical report from the police clinic where he received treatment. The judge adjourned the case until November 9 for trial and possible hearing of the bail application. The post ICPC arraigns PFIPC’s Adeyemi afresh on 22 counts appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Minerals Commission defends termination of Northern Ashanti Mines’ mineral rights over $8.3m debt
items.description: The Minerals Commission has defended its decision to terminate the mineral rights of Northern Ashanti Mines Limited, formerly Owere Mines, insisting that the company persistently failed to meet its statutory financial obligations despite several opportunities to settle its debts. According to the Commission, the company accumulated approximately US$8.33 million in unpaid Annual Mineral Right (AMR) fees on its mining leases as of April 2025, alongside US$49,928 owed on prospecting licences. Addressing a press conference, the Commission rejected allegations by Northern Ashanti Mines that the termination was carried out in bad faith, maintaining that the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources acted within his legal authority. The Commission explained that Owere Mines acquired a mining lease covering 595 cadastral blocks in January 2010 but subsequently failed to fulfil its annual payment obligations under Section 24 of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703). It disclosed that the company had accumulated more than US$4 million in outstanding fees by May 2020, prompting the issuance of a notice to remedy the breach. Press Briefing On The Revocation Of Mining Leases Of Northern Ashanti Mines Limited – October 2026 Download Following the takeover of the company by BCM Investments, management proposed settling the debt in four instalments. However, the Commission said the company failed to honour the arrangement despite being given additional opportunities. By October 2022, the outstanding debt had risen to US$5.59 million, increasing to US$6.18 million by December of the same year. The Commission indicated that further notices issued in April 2025 revealed that the company’s indebtedness had reached US$8.33 million in mining lease fees, excluding outstanding prospecting licence fees. Consequently, on April 7, 2026, the Commission recommended the termination of the company’s mineral rights to the Lands Minister, citing persistent non-payment. The Minister subsequently approved the issuance of the termination notice. Responding to the company’s challenge to the debt figures, the Commission insisted that its records showed Northern Ashanti Mines had paid only US$300,000 in two instalments, contrary to the company’s claim of having paid US$1 million. “For a company that claims to have spent US$200,000,000 on the mine, what prevented it from paying the US$8,000,000 owed to the people of Ghana?” the Commission questioned. It further criticised the company’s decision to pursue legal action against the Lands Minister, the Minerals Commission and the Attorney-General while simultaneously seeking public dialogue over the matter. The Commission maintained that the company should allow the courts to determine the dispute rather than engage in what it described as litigation through the media. It stressed that the termination of the mineral rights meant the affected concessions had reverted to the State, without cancelling the company’s outstanding financial liabilities. The Commission consequently announced its intention to pursue the recovery of all outstanding payments owed by Northern Ashanti Mines. It also emphasised the State’s responsibility to protect the affected mining assets from encroachment and other illegal activities, citing Section 70 of Act 703. The Commission reaffirmed that due process had been followed throughout the termination proceedings and insisted that no mining company, whether locally or foreign-owned, would be permitted to disregard its statutory obligations. “No one is above the law in this country. If you flout the laws, there are sanctions, and those sanctions will apply,” the Commission stated. It reiterated its commitment to enforcing Ghana’s mining laws without fear or favour, stressing that the country’s mineral resources belong to the people and must be managed in accordance with the law.

items.title: Publish details of N30bn East-West road approval, Ugolor tells Umahi
items.description: By Adesina Wahab An activist and publisher of The Common Good Letter, Rev. David Ugolor, has challenged the Minister of Works, Dave Umahi, to publish details of the Federal Government’s approval of N30 billion for remedial works on the East-West Road. Ugolor said making the details public would promote transparency and accountability in the use of public funds, while enabling communities, motorists and civil society organisations to monitor the project’s implementation. In an open letter to the minister, he welcomed the announcement that the Federal Executive Council approved the N30 billion for repairs to deteriorated sections of the road at its meeting on October 28, 2026. He, however, said the announcement should be followed by clear information on the scope of work, contractors, funding arrangements and completion timelines. “An approval is one stage of delivery. Nigerians also need to know what work has been authorised, who will execute it, how it will be financed and when it will be completed,” Ugolor said. He called on the ministry to identify all sections of the road covered by the approval, including the states, communities, kilometre points and length of each intervention. He specifically asked whether the package included the damaged Kira section in Rivers State and other locations recently affected by flooding. Ugolor also urged the ministry to publish the engineering scope, bill of quantities and completion standards, clarifying whether the funds would cover temporary repairs, permanent reconstruction, drainage improvements, bridges, culverts or road elevation. On procurement, he asked Umahi to disclose the contractors and supervising consultants, as well as whether the interventions involved new contracts, variations to existing contracts or other delivery arrangements. He further requested details of the procurement process, relevant approvals and applicable clearances from the Bureau of Public Procurement. The activist also sought clarification on the source of funding, asking the ministry to distinguish between the amount approved, funds released, payments made to contractors and sums certified against completed work, including the dates of each transaction. Ugolor called for an explanation of how the N30 billion approval related to existing East-West Road contracts and the previously announced reconstruction of approximately 400 kilometres between Edo and Cross River states. He urged the ministry to publish a consolidated schedule showing the boundaries, costs and responsibilities of the different interventions to prevent overlaps or uncertainty over project delivery. On road safety and durability, Ugolor called for the publication of relevant drainage, flood-risk and geotechnical assessments. He said the ministry should explain how the designs would address water flow, road elevation and the safety of neighbouring communities, including consultation and compensation arrangements where applicable. The publisher also asked the ministry to disclose when contractors had been or would be mobilised, the expected completion dates, measurable project milestones, traffic management arrangements and the officials responsible for monitoring progress. Ugolor urged relevant committees of the National Assembly to scrutinise the approval and track the expenditure through to the completion of the work. He also called on state governments, host communities, transport associations and civil society organisations to seek access to project information to enable them to monitor implementation. “The Common Good Letter supports urgent repairs and a transparent, adequately funded programme for the wider East-West Road,” he said. He urged Umahi to provide a consolidated public explanation accompanied by the approval, procurement, funding and implementation records. “Public money must deliver safe roads, measurable progress and lasting relief,” Ugolor added. items.title: Women domestic workers earn 48% of other employees’ wages – ILO
items.description: Women employed as domestic workers worldwide earn an average of 48% of the monthly wages of other employees, highlighting persistent gender-based inequalities in the sector, according to the International Labour Organisation (ILO). In its latest report, The State of Domestic Work in 2025: 15 Years After Convention No. 189, the ILO said women account for 77.2% of domestic workers globally and are disproportionately concentrated in cleaning and direct-care occupations. The report found that male domestic workers earn an average of 65.8% of the monthly wages of other employees, compared with 48% for their female counterparts. The figures underscore the persistent wage disparities affecting women in a sector that provides essential household services, including cleaning, cooking and caring for children, older persons and people with disabilities. The ILO estimates that 80 million people aged 15 and above are employed as domestic workers worldwide, up from 75.6 million in 2019. However, 66.5 million of these workers, representing 83.1% of the global domestic workforce, remain in informal employment, often without effective labour and social protection. The organisation said domestic workers earn an average of 53.3% of the monthly wages of other employees, while those in informal employment earn just 48.7%. The report also found that 35.2% of domestic workers work at least 49 hours per week, with 14.6% working 60 hours or more. The ILO has called for stronger implementation of its Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), and Recommendation No. 201 to improve wages, expand social protection, strengthen working-time safeguards and ensure decent working conditions. It also urged governments and other stakeholders to strengthen labour-law enforcement, promote social dialogue and collective bargaining, and invest in decent care jobs. Patrick Belser, Chief of the ILO’s Informal Work Branch, said progress in some countries showed that change was possible, but more needed to be done to address informality and the widening wage gap. “We cannot claim to value care while undervaluing the people who provide it,” he said, calling for the rights outlined in the convention to be translated into effective protection for domestic workers.

items.title: Africa records 4.2 million increase in domestic workers since 2019 – ILO
items.description: Africa recorded an increase of 4.2 million domestic workers between 2019 and 2025, the largest rise among the world’s regions, according to the International Labour Organization (ILO). However, 93.3% of domestic workers on the continent remain in informal employment, often without effective labour and social protection, the organisation has warned. The findings are contained in the ILO’s report, The State of Domestic Work in 2025: 15 Years After Convention No. 189, which examines developments in the sector since the adoption of the Domestic Workers Convention in 2011. The report indicates that the growth in Africa’s domestic workforce has occurred alongside persistent challenges in securing formal employment and adequate protection for workers. Globally, an estimated 80 million people aged 15 and above work as domestic workers, up from 75.6 million in 2019. Of this number, 66.5 million, representing 83.1% of the global domestic workforce, remain in informal employment. Domestic workers provide essential household services, including cleaning, cooking and caring for children, older persons and people with disabilities. Yet many continue to face low wages and inadequate working conditions. The ILO estimates that domestic workers worldwide earn an average of 53.3% of the monthly wages of other employees. Those in informal employment earn even less, at 48.7%. The report also found that 35.2% of domestic workers globally work at least 49 hours per week, while 14.6% work 60 hours or more. The ILO is calling for stronger implementation of its Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), and Recommendation No. 201 to expand social protection, improve wages, strengthen working-time safeguards and promote decent working conditions. It also recommends accessible worker registration, effective minimum-wage policies, stronger labour-law enforcement and greater investment in decent care jobs. The organisation says improving conditions for domestic workers will be increasingly important as demographic changes, migration and growing care needs reshape labour markets worldwide.

items.title: Départ anticipé de Christine Lagarde : la BCE à l’épreuve des visions du RN et de LFI
items.description: La presidente de la Banque centrale europeenne (BCE), Christine Lagarde, quittera ses fonctions le 7 fevrier 2027, selon un communique publie par l'institution le 29 octobre. La BCE a precise qu'elle avait informe le Conseil des gouverneurs et le president du Conseil europeen, António Costa, de sa decision. Conformement a la procedure prevue par les traites de l'Union europeenne, son successeur sera nomme par le Conseil europeen. Ce depart anticipe alimente les speculations quant a un eventuel retour de Christine Lagarde sur la scene politique francaise. Politico rapporte les propos d'un responsable proche de la presidente de la BCE, qui a affirme, sous couvert d'anonymat, qu'elle avait pris cette decision pour disposer d'« une plus grande liberte d'exprimer ses opinions et de s'engager dans des questions non monetaires, car elle ne peut rester neutre face a l'evolution de la situation dans son pays et dans le monde ». Vers de nouvelles nominations au directoire de la BCE L'annonce du depart de Christine Lagarde ouvre la voie a un accord global entre les capitales de l'Union europeenne (UE) sur au moins trois nominations au sein du directoire de la BCE, compose de six membres. Les negociations s'annoncent intenses, compte tenu du role crucial de l'institution sur les marches mondiaux et des pressions croissantes qui pesent sur les finances publiques europeennes. Parmi les candidats pressentis figurent le Neerlandais Klaas Knot, ancien gouverneur de la Banque centrale des Pays-Bas, et l'Espagnol Pablo Hernández de Cos, president de la Banque des reglements internationaux et ancien gouverneur de la Banque d'Espagne. En Allemagne, le chancelier Friedrich Merz a indique qu'une decision serait prise d'ici la fin de l'annee, rapporte Politico. L'UE tente de se premunir du risque que represente Marine Le Pen En France, le depart de Christine Lagarde permettra au president Emmanuel Macron de participer au choix de son successeur a la tete de la BCE avant la fin de son second mandat, prevue le 13 mai 2027. Alors que les sondages placent Marine Le Pen, presidente du groupe Rassemblement national (RN) a l'Assemblee nationale, parmi les personnalites en vue pour la prochaine election presidentielle, « l'UE tente de se premunir, au moins en partie, contre le risque que Marine Le Pen, candidate de droite, remporte l'election presidentielle francaise », a declare Holger Schmieding, responsable de la recherche chez Berenberg Bank, cite par Politico. La dirigeante du RN, critique de longue date de l'UE et partisane d'une « Europe des nations souveraines », pourrait avoir une conception radicalement differente du profil appele a diriger la BCE. Le chef de LFI redoute une manœuvre similaire a celle de la Banque de France De son cote, le chef de La France insoumise (LFI), Jean-Luc Melenchon, a denonce une manœuvre du president francais, qui avait deja pese sur la nomination d'un nouveau gouverneur de la Banque de France en placant son collaborateur Emmanuel Moulin a ce poste, apres le depart anticipe de Francois Villeroy de Galhau. En matiere de finances publiques, Jean-Luc Melenchon a egalement avance l'idee que la BCE se defasse de ses engagements lies a la dette francaise, une proposition largement rejetee par la droite francaise et le camp macroniste. Le successeur de Christine Lagarde devra prendre les renes de la BCE dans un contexte particulierement delicat. Les marches obligataires europeens connaissent de fortes tensions et les coûts d'emprunt atteignent des niveaux eleves sous l'effet de plusieurs facteurs : une inflation alimentee par les conflits internationaux, les evolutions demographiques et la concurrence exercee sur les marches des capitaux par les grandes entreprises technologiques, qui investissent massivement dans l'intelligence artificielle.

items.title: Rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 : la Fondation Wazni poursuit, pour la troisième année consécutive, l’accompagnement de dix jeunes filles
items.description: COMMUNIQUÉ DE PRESSE Conakry, 29 octobre 2026 – Dans le cadre du projet « Scolarisons 100 jeunes filles » , porté par la Fondation Diaka Camara, la Fondation Wazni accompagne depuis 2024 dix jeunes filles dans leur parcours scolaire et leur développement personnel. En s’associant à cette initiative, la Fondation Wazni a choisi de prendre en charge et de mentorer ces dix bénéficiaires, avec l’ambition de leur offrir les conditions nécessaires à leur réussite scolaire, à leur épanouissement et à la construction de leur avenir. À l’occasion de la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027, les dix bénéficiaires ont reçu, le 1er octobre à Conakry, leurs kits et équipements scolaires afin de débuter cette nouvelle année dans de bonnes conditions. Un accompagnement global La Fondation Wazni privilégie un accompagnement qui va au-delà de la prise en charge scolaire. Le dispositif comprend notamment la scolarité, les fournitures et les tenues scolaires, ainsi que des mesures destinées à faciliter le quotidien des bénéficiaires et à soutenir leur progression : goûter, transport, séances de révision et suivi régulier. Le programme intègre également des actions en faveur du développement personnel et de l’ouverture sur le monde professionnel, afin de permettre aux jeunes filles de découvrir de nouveaux environnements, de renforcer leurs compétences et de mieux se projeter dans leur avenir. Trois années de mentorat La poursuite de cet accompagnement en 2026-2027 marque une troisième année de mentorat auprès des dix jeunes filles. À travers un suivi régulier et personnalisé, la Fondation Wazni entend les accompagner dans leur progression, renforcer leur autonomie et les aider à construire leur projet d’avenir avec confiance. À travers sa participation au projet « Scolarisons 100 jeunes filles » , la Fondation Wazni réaffirme ainsi sa conviction que l’éducation constitue un levier essentiel d’émancipation, de développement personnel et d’accès aux opportunités. Céline Wazni, représentante de la Fondation Wazni : « Investir dans l’éducation des jeunes filles, c’est investir dans leur potentiel et dans l’avenir de toute une génération. » À propos de la Fondation Wazni La Fondation Wazni œuvre en faveur de l’éducation et du développement social à travers des initiatives visant à améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage et à favoriser l’accès des jeunes aux opportunités. Son action s’inscrit autour de sa signature : Former – Construire – Transformer.

items.title: Ghana at risk of missing 2030 methane emissions target, AMA warns, as stakeholders push for more funding and waste separation
items.description: Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) have warned, citing funding shortfalls and weak waste collection. The warning came on Wednesday at the Accra LOW-M Institutional and Climate Finance Roundtable at the Africa Regent Hotel in Accra. The event was organised by the AMA and the Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO), with the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA) and C40 Cities. It brought together the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, the Ministry of Finance, the Environmental Protection Agency and its Ghana Carbon Markets Office, the private sector and informal waste workers. Victor Kotey, the AMA’s Climate Change Focal Point, said the country was off track. “Looking at the trajectory, if we don’t put a lot more effort into this, we may not be able to achieve the 2030 [target],” he said. “If you are not getting the right investment in the right quantum, it will be very difficult to achieve this.” He said the Assembly would not be able to implement about half of the 20 priority actions in its 2020–2025 climate action plan, largely because of a lack of money. The warning comes a week after the United Nations Environment Programme’s annual Emissions Gap Report found that if current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C within this century, with methane emissions heading in the opposite direction of what countries agreed to. Ghana is among the countries backing the Global Methane Pledge, under which signatories work towards a collective effort to reduce global methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. Ghana’s waste sector commitments under its Nationally Determined Contributions include building three landfills with 50 percent methane recovery, doubling the country’s waste-to-compost capacity, and building 200 biogas facilities. Methane is produced when organic waste rots without oxygen in dumpsites and landfills. Engineer Godfred Fiifi Boadi, Head of Climate Action, Sustainability and Partnerships at the Ministry of Local Government, said that “over 20 years it is 60 to 100 times more potent than carbon dioxide”. Desmond Alugnoa, Africa Programme Manager of GAIA, said Africa as a whole is falling short. “I must admit that we are not doing as much as we could,” he said, adding that the money committed and the political will do not match what countries have promised. The roundtable centred on the Accra LOW-M (Lowering Organic Waste Methane) Portfolio, a plan to turn organic waste into compost and biogas instead of sending it to landfills. Accra aims to collect at least 50% of organic waste separately by 2030, and to divert at least 30% of organic waste by 2040. Fathia Selasi Charway-Glover, Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste Cities Project, said more than 55 percent of Accra’s waste is organic, and the plan depends on separating it at source. “We need the bylaws, we need the institutional backing from governments to ensure that this is possible,” she said. Ing. Boadi said government is building more facilities to get waste to the right places for treatment. “There is also some innovations that have been announced by the Minister for Local Government with regards to the construction of additional final disposal site facilities across the regions, and also quite a number of waste transfer stations,” he said. Mr Alugnoa said cutting food waste would also make a big difference. “If we are able to avoid the tonnage that is coming from those places by conserving our food and ensuring food security, we are also going to achieve much of our climate targets,” he said. Mr Kotey urged households to stop dumping and burning waste. “Please pay for waste collection services and make sure your waste is collected and properly treated,” he said. Ms Charway-Glover said everyone has a part to play. “If you cook and you feel like, oh, I don’t want to eat this tomorrow and you throw it away, you are part of the problem,” she said. “And so as we are part of the problem, it is the same way we need to be part of the solution.” The roundtable is expected to produce a six- to 12-month action plan for the portfolio, naming the institutions responsible for each task and setting out how it will be financed. END.

items.title: Le Financial Times refuse de rectifier son article sur l’entretien Poutine-Stubb-Store
items.description: Le Financial Times a refuse, le 29 octobre, de rectifier un article consacre a une conversation telephonique entre Vladimir Poutine, le president finlandais Alexander Stubb et le Premier ministre norvegien Jonas Gahr Store, malgre les objections des gouvernements finlandais et norvegien. Le journal britannique affirmait que le chef de l'etat russe aurait passe un temps considerable a « faire la lecon » aux deux dirigeants sur « l'histoire slave medievale » et son lien avec le conflit en Ukraine. S'appuyant sur trois sources anonymes presentees comme etant « au courant de la conversation », le Financial Times a depeint le president russe comme « obsede » par l'histoire. Le gouvernement norvegien a indique au quotidien Verdens Gang que cette description etait inexacte et que la Finlande avait contacte le Financial Times , au nom des deux pays, pour contester sa version des faits. Les medias finlandais ont egalement relaye ce dementi. De son cote, le Helsingin Sanomat , s'appuyant sur ses propres sources, a refute la description de l'entretien donnee par le journal britannique. Le Financial Times a toutefois refuse de rectifier son article, affirmant au Verdens Gang qu'il maintenait les informations publiees. Plus tard dans la journee, le conseiller du president russe, Iouri Ouchakov, a egalement dementi les informations du quotidien britannique. « Il a bien fait. C'est une information tout simplement inventee, ou plutot, ce n'est pas une information, mais de la desinformation. On n'a jamais parle de ces choses-la. Et le Premier ministre norvegien a parfaitement raison sur ce point », a-t-il commente. La conversation telephonique entre le president russe et les dirigeants finlandais et norvegien a eu lieu le 27 octobre, a l'initiative de ces derniers. a l'issue de cet echange, la partie russe a indique que les discussions avaient porte sur le reglement de la crise ukrainienne, notamment a la lumiere des entretiens de Vladimir Poutine avec Steve Witkoff, envoye special du president americain, a Saint-Petersbourg le 21 octobre, ainsi que des contacts organises a Oslo entre Alexander Stubb, Jonas Gahr Store, l'envoye americain et Volodymyr Zelensky. Les interlocuteurs ont egalement aborde les questions de securite et de stabilite dans la region de la mer Baltique et en Europe du Nord. Le president finlandais et le Premier ministre norvegien ont reaffirme l'importance du respect du droit maritime international et du principe de liberte de navigation. Le president russe a egalement informe ses interlocuteurs du lancement, sous l'egide des etats-Unis, d'une operation humanitaire dans la region d'Alechka, sous controle russe, ainsi que de l'instauration d'un « regime de silence » temporaire dans le secteur de Kherson.

items.title: The Variety Bag Has Ruined Halloween
items.description: All Halloween candy is the same now. Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home. Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next one will. A harvesttime holiday that evolved from traditional reflections on death is now merely another household chore to carry out on the way to mortal life’s certain end. In my memory, the trick-or-treating procedure used to go down like this: An older lady or stern man made some idle chatter about costumes and then dispensed one or three candies into my bag directly from their basket. The candy provided was particular and intentional: You got a Hershey’s Special Dark mini and a wee Mr. Goodbar, perhaps, or a few Smarties cylinders, or, alas, a handful of Bit-O-Honeys. Children identified houses by what they dispensed: Don’t miss the quiet bungalow that yielded a surprising payload of Rolos, but don’t bother with the big, well-manicured property on the corner where only Brach’s Jelly Nougats are on offer. Such impressions sometimes became sufficiently evocative— the Rolo house —to characterize a street’s residences at other times of the year. Not anymore. Kids’ hauls at each house are bigger than ever, but also more similar. Back when the seasonal candy was more diverse, it communicated something about the trick-or-treatee’s aesthetics and even their values. Hershey’s bars or Tootsie Roll Pops suggested traditionalism. So did shortened tubes of Necco wafers (in an esoteric way), or cellophane-wrapped, spherical hard candies (in an antiquated one). Baby Ruth or Butterfinger insinuated indulgence, moderated—Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups meant it immoderately. A miniature box of Nerds or a Blow Pop would have come across as progressive, at least during my youth. A packet of Pop Rocks would have felt positively punk rock. [ Read: A Halloween myth that can finally die ] Kids might share intelligence about the house offering Boston Baked Beans (actually good, but considered undesirable by peers) or Red Hots (symbolically righteous but actually underwhelming). A handful of Sixlets—previously unheard-of—implied a larger universe than a pre-internet child might have imagined possible. Some houses matched a kid’s unexplained taste in quiet, affirming ways. For me, Spree was a peculiar pleasure, and Chuckles jelly candies, and 3 Musketeers bars, with their gentle, whipped nougat. Some doors suggested eccentricity or extremism. Even after the razor-blade panic and Tylenol scare, some homes still gave out plastic-wrapped, homemade popcorn balls, an earnest but unwelcome attempt to retain the disappearing past. Others came off as unhinged. Dentists sometimes offered pencils or crayons instead of candy, for obvious reasons. My parents insisted on throwing handfuls of nickels into awaiting pillowcases, a practice that caused me enormous shame despite the fact that some neighborhood children appreciated it. This opportunity to express distinctiveness at the Halloween stoop, and to receive it, has become much harder. In part, that’s because trick-or-treating has declined in general. The reasons are many: The total number of trick-or-treat-age children has decreased by a quarter since 1970; community trunk-or-treats or school events in the days leading up to Halloween started supplanting the door-to-door tradition; parents and kids decamp for “better” neighborhoods, whose betterness begets ever-increasing Hallows’ Eve inequity. Neighborhoods are less connected in general, and some municipalities enforce nanny-state ordinances around the practice. But the candy has also changed. Like soda or fast food, candy was largely regional until well beyond the middle of the century. The Oh Henry! Bar, for example, was invented around 1920, by one account named after an exclamation a clerk at George Williamson’s Chicago candy store uttered to a frequent patron named Henry. But consolidation came to the candy industry. Hershey bought Reese’s in 1963, then Almond Joy and others. Mars ended up with M&M’s, Snickers, Twix, Milky Way, and many more. These days, those two companies account for around two thirds of the U.S. chocolate market. Along the way, products such as Oh Henry! fell by the wayside. That bar changed hands four times from 1965 to 2019, when it was taken off the market in the United States. Now no American child needs to ask a parent what the heck an Oh Henry! bar is, because they definitely won’t receive one in their plastic jack-o’-lantern. October retail flyers of the past reveal much greater choices. In 1970 and 1985 , Kmart advertised bags of Milk Duds, Whoppers, Dots, Sugar Daddy, Good & Plenty, and Junior Mints, among others. A 1988 coupon ad from the Leaf candy company (once the fourth-largest North American confectioner, most of whose brands were bought by Hershey in 1996) sold packs of Chuckles (my heart!), Slo Poke, Good & Fruity, Zagnut, and Rain-Blo bubble gum. Even products from companies that have survived brand acquisitions used to be more varied: Hershey’s Kisses were a common trick-or-treat offering, for example, and Tootsie Roll Industries sold bags of Tootsie Roll Pops. Now, at my local supermarket, Haribo Goldbears represent the sole independent exception. More often today, Halloween candy comes in those nefarious variety bags. This practice isn’t entirely new; a variety of Hershey’s minis—Milk Chocolate, Special Dark, Krackel, and Mr. Goodbar—were a tradition of office reception desks as much as dark neighborhoods on October 31. Now assortments are the norm. This year, I found several nearly identical Hershey’s bundles at my local Dierbergs, each containing its namesake chocolate bars along with Reese’s cups, KitKat, Almond Joy—and then an oddball from the farm leagues, such as Milk Duds, Hershey’s Cookies ‘n’ Creme, or Rolo. Reese’s Pieces, a candy that E.T. once made unique, were available only in a package with KitKat, Reese’s cups, and two types of Jolly Rancher gummies. Mars has its own versions with Snickers, Milky Way, and two kinds of M&Ms. The industrial consolidation has turned Halloween candy into an anonymous murk. That mix probably pleases every trick-or-treater a little, but it also risks making every house’s offering essentially identical. Across the street at Costco, the situation was even more dire. Enormous bags of Kirkland Signature Favorites were on offer, each containing a fusion of the other fusions: Mars and Hershey and Haribo candies all mixed together. The collection was so haphazard and homogeneous, Costco felt obliged to emblazon a large disclaimer on the packaging’s front: “This bag may not include all varieties listed.” A handful of candy an adult might dispense from the Costco superset is identical to one taken from a child’s overall plunder. The point is clear: Nobody should care what kind of treats they buy or receive anymore. All Halloween candy is what economists call a perfect substitute for other candy. Throw a bag in the cart and get the candy-having done with—then hold out the basket of whatever came in the bag and let the kiddos get the candy-taking done with too. Perhaps the indifference counts as apathy rather than disdain. Candy might just not be as important as it used to be. Changing tastes have led to an ever-widening set of options for, and conceptions of, treats: sweet beverages, frozen desserts, snack products, yogurt-alikes, breakfast cereals and bars, cookies and cakes. Sweet coffeehouse beverages, limited-edition cookies and snacks, and endless brand collaborations have also created more options and greater surface area for candy alternatives. Competition, combined with a long moral and dental disapproval of sweets, has contracted candy’s charm. [ Read: The costume I can’t persuade my husband to throw away ] Almost a decade ago, in one of the most unpopular opinions I have ever published, I wrote that full-size candy bars have no place on Halloween . My argument was that big candy bars counted as normal ones, and that Halloween (understood as a holiday of sweets rather than death) was best experienced by amassing and experiencing the treats in a novel and different form. But even all those years ago, I failed to understand how far candy bars had fallen. Full-size ones had already become unfamiliar, such that discovering them on Halloween counted as the novelty that fun-size diversity had represented. Once, a neighborhood’s children could steer one another toward the house with the Reese’s Pieces, or away from the one with the Mounds (sorry, Mounds). But now the only possible take on candy is that yours is better because it is bigger, and you are therefore better because you are more affluent: That house has full-size bars! So this year, amid the bulging plastic duffels of candy at the Costco, I found myself reconsidering the wickedness of big bars. My wife and I searched our memories of youth, ever more distant, for precedents. Big bars were rarer then, but not unheard-of. When available, we recalled, they did not typically suggest wealth but modesty matched to tribute: mostly big, plain Hershey’s bars, offered by older couples for whom the candy bore particular meaning, because Hershey had transformed chocolate from an unattainable luxury into a cheap, accessible staple. Then, just beside the anonymous mixed bag, boxes of full-size bars stacked on pallets met my eye. Costco was selling 30 to a box, with Hershey’s, Hershey’s With Almond, the Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup two pack, and the four-fingered KitKat. Even the full-size bars had been relegated to an assortment.

items.title: NPP rejects reports of changes to Minority leadership in parliament
items.description: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) has rejected reports that it is considering changes to its parliamentary leadership, saying no discussions have taken place to replace Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin and his team. The party’s General Secretary, Justin Kodua Frimpong, said the NPP was satisfied with the current leadership of the Minority Caucus and had no plans to reshuffle the team. Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, October 29, he accused those spreading the reports of attempting to create divisions within the party’s parliamentary ranks. “Let me state it categorically. The party has never had any meeting. The party has never thought about even deliberating to change the leadership in Parliament. We have not,” he said. Mr Kodua Frimpong added that those seeking to create confusion among the parliamentary leadership and the Minority Caucus would not succeed. Meanwhile, he has cautioned party members seeking to position themselves as running mate to the NPP’s flagbearer for the 2028 general election through social media campaigns. He said the party’s constitution does not provide for the selection of a running mate through a competitive process or public campaigning. According to him, the decision rests with the party’s flagbearer in consultation with the National Council. “There is nowhere in our constitution which says that the running mate is selected through a contest or through a campaign; so the people who are busily urging bloggers to promote themselves, you are wrong,” he said.

items.title: GAYO, AMA hold roundtable to secure funding and institutional backing for Accra’s methane reduction plan
items.description: The Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) and the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) have held a roundtable to get government institutions and funders to commit to Accra’s plan to cut methane emissions from waste. The Accra LOW-M Institutional and Climate Finance Roundtable: Advancing Coordinated Action and Climate Finance for Urban Methane Reduction, held on Wednesday at the Africa Regent Hotel in Accra, focused on the Accra LOW-M (Lowering Organic Waste Methane) Portfolio. The plan aims to cut methane emissions from the city’s waste by at least 30 percent by 2030, mainly by turning organic waste into compost and biogas instead of sending it to landfills. The meeting, co-organised with the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives (GAIA) and C40 Cities, brought together the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, the Ministry of Finance, the Environmental Protection Agency and its Ghana Carbon Markets Office, the private sector and informal waste workers. Fathia Selasi Charway-Glover, Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste Cities Project, said the aim was to get each institution to take responsibility for its part of the plan. “Today, we are essentially here to bring together all institutions across government offices and across the roles of each of these institutions when it comes to the implementation of the portfolio,” she said. She explained that LOW-M is a global initiative supported by the Climate and Clean Air Coalition. It was launched at COP28 to encourage cities to set targets for reducing organic waste and methane by 2030. She said more than 55 percent of Accra’s waste is organic, and that the plan depends on separating it at source. Desmond Alugnoa, Africa Programme Manager of GAIA, said the portfolio was designed to bring scattered efforts under one plan. “This is to help coordinate all the implementation activities that are happening within the city and beyond the city,” he said. He added that informal waste workers would be central to educating households on separating their waste, and that he was looking to the Ministry of Finance to commit budget to collection, composting and biogas. The AMA says it needs that support. Victor Kotey, the Assembly’s Climate Change Focal Point, said waste management is expensive and the Assembly cannot raise enough revenue on its own. “Investment is a problem in the waste sector and in the other sectors as well,” he said. He warned that without more effort and money, Ghana may not meet its 2030 target. Engineer Godfred Fiifi Boadi, Head of Climate Action, Sustainability and Partnerships at the Ministry of Local Government, said the plan builds on existing national efforts, including compost plants, biogas facilities and faecal sludge treatment plants. “There are many interventions across the country that helps to divert this organic waste from actually entering landfills,” he said. The roundtable is expected to produce four outcomes: a responsibility matrix naming the lead institution and focal person for each action, a six- to 12-month action plan, a pipeline of projects seeking funding, and a tracker to monitor commitments made at the meeting. Organisers say the outcomes will be shared with participants in early November, with follow-up on commitments through to December. END.

items.title: Le Sénégal entend intégrer les technologies spatiales à ses politiques publiques pour renforcer sa souveraineté
items.description: Faire des technologies spatiales un levier de souverainete et de renforcement des politiques publiques dans plusieurs secteurs : telle est l'ambition du gouvernement senegalais et du president Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Cette strategie vise a mettre les applications spatiales au service de l'agriculture, de la peche, de la prevention des inondations, de l'amenagement du territoire et de la securite. Elle s'appuie notamment sur des projets d'infrastructures astronomiques, d'assemblage de satellites, de mobilite urbaine, de telemedecine et de surveillance du territoire. C'est ce qui ressort des propos tenus par Maram Kaïre, directeur general de l'Agence senegalaise d'etudes spatiales (ASES), en marge d'un atelier de vulgarisation des sciences spatiales destine aux medias et aux leaders religieux, organise du 26 au 28 octobre 2026 a Toubab Dialaw, dans l'ouest du Senegal. Soulignant la necessite de faire de l'ambition spatiale un projet national a part entiere, le responsable de l'ASES a declare : « Il etait important pour nous de faire en sorte que non seulement les medias comprennent de quoi il s'agit quand nous parlons de sciences spatiales, mais que la societe s'approprie egalement le projet de developpement spatial que nous avons ». Enrichir l'« ADN » de l'economie grâce aux technologies spatiales Maram Kaïre a souligne l'importance des ressources maritimes dans l'economie senegalaise. La technologie satellitaire constitue ainsi un atout majeur pour preserver les ressources halieutiques, proteger les installations petrolieres offshore et lutter contre les activites illicites dans les eaux du pays. « Notre economie devrait avoir, dans le futur, dans son ADN meme, l'utilisation des technologies spatiales pour s'enrichir », a-t-il plaide, appelant a integrer progressivement ces technologies dans les activites economiques. L'ASES envisage plusieurs projets structurants. Parmi les plus importants figure la construction de l'un des principaux observatoires de recherche en astronomie et en astrophysique d'Afrique de l'Ouest, ainsi que la creation du premier institut national d'astrophysique, qui devrait contribuer a diversifier les filieres scientifiques proposees aux etudiants senegalais. Sur le plan industriel, la creation d'un centre d'assemblage de microsatellites et de nanosatellites permettrait de developper les capacites nationales dans ce domaine. Dans cette perspective, l'Agence senegalaise d'etudes spatiales travaille avec l'etat-major general des armees au lancement de deux satellites : le premier serait destine a la surveillance maritime et le second a celle des frontieres, afin de renforcer la securite du territoire. Accords Artemis : renforcer les competences des ingenieurs et techniciens En adherant, en juillet 2025, aux accords Artemis, qui s'inscrivent dans le cadre de la cooperation internationale autour de l'exploration spatiale, le Senegal entend tirer parti de nouvelles perspectives de formation et de montee en competences pour ses ingenieurs et techniciens du secteur spatial. Maram Kaïre a indique que des specialistes senegalais avaient recemment ete sollicites pour soumettre des propositions de robots ou de dispositifs techniques susceptibles d'etre utilises sur la Lune. Cette initiative permettrait au pays de contribuer activement au projet, au-dela d'une simple participation institutionnelle. « Nous ne voulons pas etre des spectateurs, nous voulons etre des acteurs », a-t-il souligne.
