items.title: Édouard Philippe, candidat à la présidentielle française, ressort le « bras de fer » avec l’Algérie
items.description: Pas sûr d'accéder au second tour, le candidat du centre à l'élection présidentielle française de 2027, Édouard Philippe , actionne le levier de l’Algérie et de l’immigration et fait de la surenchère. Constat d' « échec de l'intégration depuis plusieurs décennies », « surreprésentation » des jeunes issus de l’immigration lors des dernières émeutes qui ont secoué la France samedi 17 octobre, promesse de réduire l’immigration légale de moitié, de restreindre le regroupement familial et de dénoncer l'accord franco-algérien de 1968 sur l’immigration. Dans une interview au Point, l’ancien Premier ministre d’Emmanuel Macron a tenu des propos difficiles à distinguer de la rhétorique de l’extrême-droite. Immigration en France : pour Édouard Philippe, l'échec de l’intégration est “ incontestable ” “ Lors des violences du 17 octobre, la surreprésentation de jeunes issus de l'immigration était patente. (…) L'échec de l'intégration dans notre pays depuis plusieurs décennies est incontestable ”, a déclaré le chef du parti Horizons. Et voici ce qu'il promet de faire s’il est élu au printemps prochain concernant l’immigration : “Je veux, au cours du prochain quinquennat, diviser l'immigration légale par deux en limitant la délivrance de titres de séjour aux seuls motifs professionnels et aux étudiants, restreindre le regroupement familial, réformer l'instruction de l'asile ”. Édouard Philippe promet de durcir le “ bras de fer ” avec l’Algérie Édouard Philippe n'oublie pas l’Algérie, devenue objet de surenchère électorale d’une large frange de la classe politique française. Le candidat a promis de “ durcir le bras de fer avec les pays d'origine (de l’immigration, ndlr), et notamment avec l'Algérie en dénonçant le traité de 1968 ”. Philippe était l'un des tout premiers à soutenir l’idée de révocation de l'accord de 1968 lancée en 2023 par Xavier Driencourt, ancien ambassadeur en Algérie. Imane Bounouh répond à Édouard Philippe : “ On ne sera pas le cache-nez de votre xénophobie ” Imane Bounouh, élue municipale de gauche au Mans, a répondu à Édouard Philippe sur Instagram. “ Il dit en parlant des jeunes du 17 octobre que c’est le signe de l'échec de l’intégration. Là où nous, on voit des Français, lui il voit des Noirs et des Arabes ”, a dit l'élue et influenceuse d'origine algérienne et marocaine. Dans l’interview, Philippe a indiqué que l’échec de l’intégration “ ne minimise en aucun cas certaines superbes réussites d'intégration républicaine ”. Pour Imane Bounouh, cette phrase est juste destinée à “ alléger ” le “ propos xénophobe ” du candidat à la présidentielle. “ On n’est pas vos très beaux exemples d’intégration républicaine et on ne sera pas les cautions de votre système qui ne marche pas. Et surtout, on ne sera pas le cache-nez de votre xénophobie et de votre racisme ”, lui a-t-elle rétorqué. Le post d’Imane Bounouh a été partagé sur X par la championne de basket Emilie Gomis. Imane Bounouh élue au Mans https://t.co/PXqX1ckAiZ — Emilie Gomis (@emiliegomis) October 28, 2026 L’article Édouard Philippe, candidat à la présidentielle française, ressort le « bras de fer » avec l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Polluted priorities
items.description: LAHORE is choking again, and the government’s answer is to send more machines onto its streets. On Wednesday, its air quality index reached 296 , putting children, outdoor workers, and the elderly at particular risk. Yet Punjab plans to acquire 30 more truck-mounted fog cannons. These can suppress road dust locally, but their ability to reduce the fine particles most harmful to health remains questionable. Authorities must explain what the existing fleet has achieved in terms of measurable pollution reduction before spending more public money. Last year, disruptions to Punjab’s air monitoring network raised suspicions that pollution levels were being hidden; officials cited technical faults. Whether equipment is recording pollution or spraying water, public confidence depends on transparent data and independent scrutiny. A temporary improvement at a pollution hotspot, or near a monitoring station, cannot prove that the city’s air is becoming safer. Monitoring should expose pollution. Punjab must publish continuous readings and independent assessments of its interventions. It should also fund research into the relative contributions of traffic, industry, construction, and crop burning, how these change with the seasons, and which measures actually reduce exposure. That scientific effort must extend beyond the border. Punjab officials say easterly winds have been bringing polluted air from India into Lahore. But this does not absolve Pakistan of responsibility for its own emissions. The air over the two Punjabs is shared, and both populations suffer when political hostility obstructs cooperation. Calls for joint action are not new. Cooperation was proposed with Indian Punjab in 2017 and 2024. Yet neither initiative led to sustained cooperation. Environmental diplomacy with New Delhi should be prioritised, despite wider tensions. Both sides could begin by exchanging verified air-quality and weather data, jointly studying the movement of pollutants and developing common approaches to agricultural burning and industrial emissions. Universities and scientific institutions could help build a shared evidence base. At home, dedicated research funding, stronger monitoring, and open evaluation of anti-smog spending are essential. Enforcement must continue, but decisions should follow evidence, not the visibility of machinery on city roads. Until the air itself improves, no amount of official activity can be called progress. Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

items.title: Can Democracy Survive the Next Financial Crash?
items.description: T he bailout clock is ticking. In September, Oracle invoked “force majeure” to delay paying debt on a data center, which led to a drop in the corporation’s stock price. This month, OpenAI significantly cut its revenue projections; CoreWeave, a heavily leveraged data-center company, saw its share price plunge; and investors began racing to buy credit-default swaps to protect their portfolios. These are all signs of declining investor confidence. The risk that the heavily debt-fueled and interconnected AI sector could crash—taking the broader economy with it—is high and rising. When the next crash happens, originating from whatever sector, the president will control a bailout apparatus with essentially limitless authority. Ever since the 2008 global financial crisis, the Federal Reserve and U.S. Treasury have claimed, with almost no resistance, more power to deal with each successive financial emergency. These bailouts were rationalized on the basis that they were in the public interest and at least theoretically subject to congressional oversight. But if the crash happens on Donald Trump’s watch , his administration would likely sidestep Congress entirely. A Trump bailout would proceed on whatever terms please the president and his allies, who would use it as a bonanza to enrich their favored companies and CEOs, even if they were the ones who caused the crisis to begin with. The billionaires—and the trillionaire—in Trump’s inner circle have already usurped decision making about which federal agencies to decimate, which federal workers to fire, which scientific research to defund, and which industries to deem necessary for national security. They could also usurp the bailout apparatus, making it spin into action even before a crisis arrives. When they start feeling financially wobbly, they might go to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, or, most likely, Trump himself and request an emergency declaration to justify a bailout. They would know that the current Supreme Court majority would be unlikely to block an emergency declaration by the executive branch and central bank. [ Annie Lowr ] ey: The AI bubble is no ordinary bubble The bailout authority is a loaded gun. Once triggered, it would bring downsides that have become familiar since 2008: public deficits and debt that devour GDP, zombie companies that taxpayers are forced to carry, an expansion of wealth inequality, and a dramatic shift of losses from perpetrators to the public. In Trump’s hands, it would also feature a new and more frightening dynamic: the creation of a standing money printer that can be turned on for the president’s allies and turned off for his enemies, enabling state-supported favoritism and plunder on a staggering scale. H istorically, the rationale for a bailout was that central banks should play the role of what Walter Bagehot called the “lender of last resort,” extending loans as necessary to tide over a blameless firm—a firm that, but for circumstances beyond its control, would otherwise be solvent and able to post adequate collateral. In 1932, Congress put this function inside the Federal Reserve. Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act gave the central bank the power to extend loans to banks and any corporate entity in “unusual and exigent circumstances.” During the Great Depression, the Fed made limited use of its new authority. Then, for seven decades, Section 13(3) sat idle. The 2008 crash inaugurated the modern bailout era. When that crisis hit, its scale was unprecedented; financial markets had grown, becoming more intertwined and complex. The Federal Reserve, under Chairman Ben Bernanke, deemed the situation “urgent and exigent” and used Section 13(3) to establish special-purpose vehicles to buy up financial assets. Section 13(3) was also used to justify loans to AIG, an insurance company, and its affiliates, in exchange for collateral that consisted of nonperforming financial instruments with dubious market value. Working closely with the Treasury, which had related legal authority under the vague goal of dollar stability, the Federal Reserve began a program of extending loans to banks and other financial firms while purchasing huge quantities of mortgages and other shaky assets held by such entities as credit-card companies and private student-loan lenders. I served as a Federal Reserve governor during the tail end of the financial crisis, and then as the deputy secretary of the Treasury in the Obama administration. I eventually came to see that the bailout of the financial sector was not doing much for the broader economy. Long after the financial sector had recovered, many Americans were out of work, unable to repay their mortgages, and contending with rapacious debt collectors and sloppy mortgage servicers. Ordinary people could not help themselves to the enormous sampling of bailout options that the Federal Reserve and Treasury had provided to the banks. Mortgage-relief programs were slow to get off the ground and undermined by arguments that the intended recipients never should have had access to subprime loans in the first place. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act, a financial-reform bill, in part to address the distributional consequences of what had just happened and to limit the Federal Reserve’s emergency powers. Ultimately, however, the law left largely intact the Fed’s discretion to choose bailout recipients, the interest rate charged on bailout loans, and the quality and value of the collateral taken to backstop those loans. A decade later, when the coronavirus pandemic threatened an economic slowdown, the Federal Reserve mobilized preemptively. It initiated an even more aggressive version of large-scale asset purchases, with earlier money and more of it. Chairman Jerome Powell’s bailout opened up all of the faucets that spurt out continuous liquidity and created some new ones. Expanding its usage of Section 13(3) beyond mortgage assets, the Fed purchased the debts of various companies. In many cases, no requirements were imposed on these firms in exchange for cheap financing. By the Federal Reserve’s own estimates, the highly indebted fossil-fuel industry, for example, reaped more than $1.47 billion from the Main Street Lending Program—8.4 percent of the allocated funds—after lobbying the Fed to make the terms of its loans more generous. The Fed’s purchases of this debt “took all the risk overhang you normally associate with a risky company and took it off the table,” one chief investment officer told The Wall Street Journal at the time. By the time Silicon Valley Bank suddenly failed, in 2023, the Federal Reserve had learned that it could bail out favored sectors without imposing any consequences on failed businesses. Even though no one would have described this midsize regional bank as a “too big to fail” institution, the Federal Reserve and Treasury drew on the techniques they had perfected during the financial crisis and the pandemic. They established the Bank Term Funding Program to lend against collateral with depressed values. Interest rates were set so low as to permit any eligible entity to borrow from the Fed rather than the private sector, even after the threat of any deposit run had subsided. The result of these three bailouts was a collective recognition that the Federal Reserve had the power to choose winners and losers. Big banks and oil companies could be winners, the crypto sector and Silicon Valley–backed venture firms could be winners, and the CEOs and owners of these entities could be winners—even if they had acted recklessly. Families who had lost their homes and their incomes would be losers; so would entrepreneurs who aspired to displace companies that, but for a bailout, would have gone under. This approach widened income and wealth inequality, further shrinking the middle class. The companies that had been bailed out continued to act in ways that had permitted them to shed their costs to the public. In each case, these bailouts were conducted hastily, because of the unchallenged view that allowing companies or sectors to collapse would deprive the economy of necessary public benefits. And they were conducted with little consideration of their long-term consequences. T he recent history of bailouts gives us a clear indication of what the next one will look like. Enormous public money will be spent, in magnitudes approaching or exceeding the amount that Congress appropriates as part of its fiscal functions. The Federal Reserve and Treasury will once again choose the sectors that will benefit, and the terms on which bailouts will be offered. Only this time, the process will be under the aegis of an administration that brazenly trades political favors for money and support. The government could buy up nonperforming debt from favored firms; more nonperforming debt could be unloaded by data-center financiers and family foundations headed by allies of the president. Once the bailout machine is turned on, businesses will line up to buy favorable terms in exchange for political contributions. Those that refuse to play this game would be left to fail. [ Listen: On the brink of global recession ] But this chaotic free-for-all is not inevitable. Congress created the government’s bailout powers, and Congress can constrain them. If it does not, then it will be implicated in the consequences. If no public benefit justifies reviving a failing firm, then Congress should allow it to fail. If failing companies are going to be rescued, then conditions must be attached to bailout funds to make sure that the public benefit will be achieved. Congress should structure these terms before the next bailout. If the businesses being bailed out are data centers, for example, Congress could require them to limit their emissions or build their own renewable-energy sources. If the businesses being bailed out are the creators of frontier AI models, they could be required to prioritize investments in medical research. To make these judgments, Congress could establish a bailout manager to identify the public benefit, establish the conditions needed for the benefit to be delivered, and then oversee adherence to those conditions long after the crisis has passed. Every bailout is a sign of economic failure. Without interventions by our elected representatives, future bailouts won’t just risk widening inequality—they stand to politicize our entire economic system. A president who wields the bailout gun on his own behalf could leave the country with societal damage that will take generations to remediate. It’s up to Congress to assess those dangers now and determine how to intervene, while it still has the chance.

items.description: Former US president Barack Obama on Wednesday mocked President Donald Trump for mobilising a government-wide response to his earlier remark that Trump had “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory ”. “The White House even called the Secretary of Treasury,” Obama remarked, as he continued his campaign ahead of the congressional races in the US. Obama quipped, “This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who’s supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable… They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.” Trump defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated. “The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” Trump said in Ohio. Neither man is on the ballot, but Republican President Trump and Democratic former president Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Wednesday, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington. While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering speeches criticising Trump. Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close. On Wednesday, Obama appeared in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces a challenge from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican. While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America’s values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta. “There is a moral component to the choices we face right now,” Obama said. “We are not going to fix the system that’s broken, we’re not going to unrig our economy, so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth,” Obama said. Trump’s public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war , but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout. Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022. Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the president appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown. Trump attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies the president said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. “The town went to hell,” he said. Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations local officials repeatedly said were untrue. Trump faces protesters Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined Trump’s motorcade route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners that read, “Republican against Trump,” “Grab them by the ballot” and “GOP: Guardians of pedophiles.” During the rally, protesters interrupted Trump several times, including at least one who shouted about deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said in response. Trump and Epstein socialised in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s private club in Palm Beach, Florida. Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump, as well as many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated. Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security. Alaska, Michigan races Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate. The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan. Representatives for Peltola did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did,” Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio. In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energise supporters and boost turnout. Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit.

items.title: Ouganda : Aider aussi ceux qui accueillent
items.description: © Internet En Ouganda, le programme DRDIP a financé des écoles, des centres de santé et des activités économiques pour les réfugiés et leurs communautés d’accueil. Une seconde phase, annoncée pour octobre 2026, doit prolonger ces investissements. Dans le district de Moyo, Leya, réfugiée sud-soudanaise et mère de cinq enfants, a développé une activité de couture grâce à une formation et à une subvention de 6 000 dollars. Ses revenus lui ont ensuite permis d’acheter une terre agricole pour contribuer à nourrir sa famille, rapporte la Banque mondiale. Son parcours s’inscrit dans le programme DRDIP, lancé en 2017 par le gouvernement avec l’appui de l’institution. Déployé dans quinze districts accueillant des réfugiés, le dispositif associe les réfugiés et les communautés locales au choix des investissements et au suivi des réalisations. Les activités soutenues comprennent l’agriculture, l’élevage, la formation professionnelle et les petites entreprises. Des groupes d’épargne et des fonds villageois facilitent également l’accès aux ressources. Selon le bilan publié le 19 mars 2026, les ménages participants ont enregistré des revenus annuels supérieurs de plus de 17% à ceux des non-participants. Services sociaux de base Les investissements concernent aussi les équipements utilisés quotidiennement. Entre 2017 et 2024, 290 écoles ont été construites ou améliorées, au bénéfice de plus de 490 000 élèves. La construction ou la réhabilitation de 130 centres de santé a également renforcé l’offre de soins. La Banque mondiale rapporte une progression de 47% des inscriptions dans le primaire dans les zones ciblées et une diminution de 36% des dépenses annuelles de santé des bénéficiaires. Les infrastructures servent aux réfugiés comme aux populations locales. D’autres financements ont accompagné l’intégration des services dans les dispositifs publics. Un programme de transferts budgétaires aux collectivités a notamment permis de rattacher 51 écoles primaires et 15 centres de santé, auparavant gérés par des partenaires humanitaires, aux systèmes nationaux. Les populations réfugiées ont été intégrées à la formule de financement local de ces services. Un mécanisme suit aussi les nouveaux afflux de réfugiés pour financer les écoles, les centres de santé et les points d’eau les plus sollicités. Des chantiers restent toutefois inachevés, ont souligné des parlementaires le 15 septembre. Le pays subit également les coupes de l’aide alimentaire rappelées par le Programme alimentaire mondial le 2 octobre. Prévue sur cinq ans, la deuxième phase du DRDIP dispose d’une enveloppe annoncée de 328 millions de dollars. Elle cible trois millions de réfugiés et de membres des communautés d’accueil dans quatorze districts, avec des investissements dans les services publics, les activités économiques et l’environnement.

items.title: Embargo américain contre Cuba : le Gabon vote pour la levée des sanctions
items.description: À l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, le Gabon s’est prononcé en faveur de la résolution réclamant la levée de l’embargo américain contre Cuba. Adopté dans un contexte de tensions entre Washington et La Havane, le texte recueille un soutien international en recul, alors que l’île fait face à de graves pénuries économiques et énergétiques. L'Assemblée générale des Nations Unies adopte une résolution réclamant la levée de l’embargo imposé par les États-Unis à Cuba. © ONU Photos Le Gabon a voté en faveur de la levée de l’embargo économique, commercial et financier imposé à Cuba par les États-Unis. Mercredi 28 octobre 2026, à New York, l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies a une nouvelle fois appelé Washington à mettre fin à ces sanctions, en vigueur depuis plus de six décennies. Si le texte réaffirme une position défendue par de nombreux États, le scrutin de cette année révèle néanmoins un recul du soutien international à La Havane. Présentée par Cuba, la résolution exhorte également les autres pays à ne pas appliquer de mesures similaires, jugées contraires aux principes de la Charte des Nations unies. Elle dénonce notamment les effets extraterritoriaux de la loi Helms-Burton de 1996, qui permet de sanctionner certaines activités économiques étrangères liées à l’île. Le texte a recueilli 130 voix favorables, contre 17 oppositions et 25 abstentions. En 2025, il avait obtenu 165 voix pour, tandis qu’en 2024, 187 pays s’étaient prononcés en faveur de la levée de l’embargo. Le vote du Gabon s’inscrit ainsi dans la continuité de la position défendue par les États favorables à la fin des sanctions américaines. Une crise économique et humanitaire aggravée Le détail des votes. © ONU Photos Cette mobilisation diplomatique intervient alors que Cuba subit de graves difficultés économiques et énergétiques. Le durcissement des mesures américaines sous Donald Trump, notamment les menaces de droits de douane visant les pays fournisseurs de pétrole, accentue les tensions sur l’approvisionnement de l’île. Les coupures d’électricité perturbent les transports, la distribution d’eau et le fonctionnement des hôpitaux. Des responsables onusiens ont également alerté sur les conséquences sanitaires de la crise, avec plus de 100 000 interventions chirurgicales reportées signalées en mai Pour le représentant du Mexique, l’embargo constitue un obstacle structurel au développement cubain. « Mettre un terme à ce blocus est une urgente nécessité » , a-t-il insisté. Le Ghana a, pour sa part, dénoncé des sanctions « iniques » , appelant à un règlement négocié du différend. Washington et La Havane à couteaux tirés Le débat a également été marqué par une vive altercation entre l’ambassadeur américain auprès de l’ONU, Mike Waltz, et le ministre cubain des Affaires étrangères, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla. Le diplomate américain a contesté l’existence même d’un blocus, mettant en avant les exportations américaines vers Cuba. La Havane accuse, au contraire, Washington de mener une politique d’asphyxie économique. Si la résolution adoptée exprime une nouvelle fois la désapprobation d’une majorité d’États, elle reste non contraignante. La levée de l’embargo relève du Congrès américain. Le vote du Gabon marque donc une prise de position diplomatique, sans effet immédiat sur les sanctions qui continuent de peser sur l’économie et la population cubaines. L’article Embargo américain contre Cuba : le Gabon vote pour la levée des sanctions est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Soupçonné d’infidélité, il tue sa compagne de 26 ans
items.description: Une jeune femme de 26 ans a été retrouvée morte à son domicile, le mercredi 28 octobre 2026, au quartier Kennedy 2 de Daloa, en Côte d’Ivoire. Son compagnon, un employé de boulangerie du même âge, soupçonné de l’avoir mortellement frappée avec une bouteille à la suite d’une dispute liée à des soupçons d’infidélité, a été interpellé par la Brigade de recherche et d’intervention (BRI). L’information a été rendue publique, ce jeudi 29 octobre, par la plate-forme ivoirienne Police Secours. Le quartier Kennedy 2 de Daloa a été le théâtre d’un drame conjugal aux conséquences tragiques. Aux environs de 6 heures du matin, le mercredi 28 octobre 2026, le corps sans vie de D. L. Fabienne, âgée de 26 ans, a été découvert dans le salon de son domicile, baignant dans une mare de sang. Gérante d’un maquis, la jeune femme partageait un logement de deux pièces avec son compagnon, S. Arthur, également âgé de 26 ans et employé dans une boulangerie. Alertés, les éléments de la Brigade de recherche et d’intervention (BRI) de Daloa, appuyés par des agents du commissariat du 2ᵉ arrondissement et de la Police scientifique et technique, se sont rendus sur les lieux pour les premières constatations. L’examen du corps a révélé une blessure à la tête. Le médecin dépêché sur place a confirmé le décès et évoqué un violent coup porté à la tempe à l’aide d’un objet. Une dispute sur fond de soupçons d’infidélité Les investigations policières se sont rapidement orientées vers le compagnon de la victime. Interpellé puis entendu par les enquêteurs, S. Arthur a livré sa version des faits. Selon les déclarations rapportées par Police Secours, une dispute aurait éclaté entre les deux partenaires en raison de soupçons d’infidélité. La querelle aurait ensuite dégénéré en altercation physique. Au cours de celle-ci, le suspect aurait saisi une bouteille pour frapper violemment sa compagne à la tempe. Toujours selon le récit qu’il aurait livré aux enquêteurs, la jeune femme aurait succombé à ses blessures quelques heures plus tard. Le compagnon, qui aurait reconnu les faits lors de son interrogatoire, a été interpellé par les éléments de la BRI de Daloa. Le procureur de la République a été informé du drame, tandis que l’enquête a été confiée à cette unité de police afin de déterminer avec précision les circonstances du décès. La jalousie, une nouvelle fois au cœur d’un drame conjugal La mort de Fabienne, à seulement 26 ans, rappelle les conséquences dramatiques que peuvent engendrer les violences au sein du couple. Une dispute amoureuse, des soupçons ou la jalousie ne sauraient justifier le recours à la violence, encore moins la perte d’une vie humaine. Désormais entre les mains de la justice, le suspect devra répondre des faits qui lui sont reprochés, au terme de la procédure judiciaire. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Soupçonné d’infidélité, il tue sa compagne de 26 ans est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Série de mesures au ministère de la santé pour la mise en service des nouveaux centres de santé nouvellement créés
items.description: Le ministère de la Santé a entamé les préparatifs en vue de la mise en service des nouveaux centres de santé à Nouakchott, en veillant à ce que les besoins en approvisionnement soient comblés, en renforçant le suivi sur le terrain et en améliorant la préparation des équipes sanitaires. La ministre de la Santé, Naha Hamdi Mouknass, a tenu une réunion consacrée au suivi de l’avancement des préparatifs, en présence du secrétaire général du ministère, des membres du comité de supervision, des directeurs régionaux de la santé des trois wilayas de Nouakchott, ainsi que de représentants de la centrale d’achat des médicaments et des fournitures médicales et du secteur de la transformation numérique et de la modernisation de l’administration. La ministre a chargé la centrale d’achat de médicaments et de matériel médical de garantir l’approvisionnement des nouveaux centres, le système de ravitaillement adopté devant faire l’objet d’une évaluation trois mois après sa mise en œuvre, afin d’en mesurer l’efficacité et d’y apporter les améliorations nécessaires. Le ministère a également mis en place un mécanisme de suivi quotidien, en chargeant un responsable du ministère de suivre chaque centre, de surveiller l’avancement des travaux et des préparatifs, et de remettre des rapports quotidiens à la commission de supervision, ce qui permettra de remédier aux lacunes avant la mise en service de ces centres. S’agissant des ressources humaines, la formation destinée au personnel des nouveaux centres qui débutera jeudi alliera formation théorique et formation pratique sur le terrain, dans le but de renforcer la préparation des agents et de les former aux exigences du travail au sein de ces établissements, a annoncé le ministère de la Santé.

items.title: Ecobuilders MS défend les couleurs du Sénégal à la compétition régionale
items.description: Lauréate du premier prix de la compétition nationale IYBA-SEED, le 21 octobre dernier, l’entreprise Ecobuilders MS, fondée par l’ingénieure civile Ndèye Marie Aida Ndiéguène, sera en lice ce 29 octobre pour la compétition régionale dédiée à l’expansion des entreprises vertes dirigées par des femmes. Le Sénégal y affrontera quatre autres pays : le Bénin, le Kenya, l’Afrique du Sud et le Togo. Le rendez-vous est fixé à ce jeudi 29 octobre. Après avoir remporté le premier prix de la compétition nationale IYBA-SEED, le 21 octobre dernier, Ecobuilders MS s’apprête à franchir une nouvelle étape de son parcours. L’entreprise, spécialisée dans la construction durable, l’économie circulaire et l’innovation agricole, représentera le Sénégal à la compétition régionale consacrée à l’expansion des entreprises vertes dirigées par des femmes. Lire aussi: Ndeye Marie Aida Ndiéguène, fondatrice d’Ecobuilders Ms: « Tant que chaque producteur n’aura pas un I3S, je ne serai pas satisfaite » (2/2) À la tête de cette structure, l’ingénieure civile Ndèye Marie Aida Ndiéguène entend porter les ambitions de son entreprise au-delà des frontières nationales. Pour la fondatrice, cette distinction est une « immense fierté », mais aussi une « profonde source d’émotion et de motivation ». Derrière cette récompense, elle voit l’aboutissement de plusieurs années d’efforts. « Derrière cette distinction, il y a des années de travail, de sacrifices, de persévérance et surtout une conviction inébranlable : celle que nous pouvons construire un avenir plus durable à partir de nos propres ressources et de nos innovations », souligne-t-elle. Avec Ecobuilders MS, l’entrepreneure mise sur l’écoconstruction, la valorisation des déchets et l’économie circulaire comme leviers de transformation. Une démarche qui, selon elle, démontre que les initiatives locales peuvent contribuer à bâtir un modèle de développement plus respectueux de l’environnement. Un engagement au-delà des frontières La participation à la compétition régionale représente ainsi un enjeu important pour l’entreprise sénégalaise. En lice avec des structures venues du Bénin, du Kenya, d’Afrique du Sud et du Togo, Ecobuilders MS aura l’occasion de mettre en avant son approche de la construction durable et de l’économie circulaire, tout en défendant son potentiel de développement sur les marchés régionaux. Pour Ndèye Marie Aida Ndiéguène, cette reconnaissance s’accompagne d’un sens accru des responsabilités. « Représenter le Sénégal à l’échelle régionale est un honneur, mais aussi un engagement : celui de porter haut les couleurs de notre pays et de démontrer que les entreprises vertes africaines ont leur place parmi les acteurs qui façonnent le monde de demain », affirme-t-elle. Au Sénégal, le programme IYBA-SEED vise à contribuer à la construction d’un écosystème entrepreneurial durable, en s’attaquant aux difficultés structurelles qui freinent le développement des entreprises dirigées par les jeunes et les femmes. Il entend notamment améliorer les services d’accompagnement proposés aux entrepreneurs et renforcer la coopération entre les acteurs du secteur. Pour la fondatrice d’Ecobuilders MS, le prix national obtenu le 21 octobre ne constitue pas une finalité, mais plutôt un tremplin. « C’est une nouvelle étape, un encouragement à aller plus loin, à innover davantage et à continuer de bâtir un avenir où développement économique et préservation de l’environnement avancent ensemble. » Arame NDIAYE

items.title: Déplacés : L’aide reçue ne suffit pas
items.description: © Internet Après les attaques de septembre, Médecins sans frontières (MSF) a alerté le 20 octobre 2026 sur les besoins des déplacés de Macina. Les témoignages et les réponses recueillis par Journal du Mali racontent une assistance confrontée au manque de ressources, aux difficultés d’accès et à la persistance des besoins. À Ségou, Mama Follé et Ba Oumou Diarra ont reçu des vivres et des kits non alimentaires. Originaires de Founou, dans le cercle de Ké-Macina, elles racontent avoir fui l’insécurité sans pouvoir emporter leurs biens. L’alimentation et les abris restent leurs priorités. Toutes deux saluent les autorités et les humanitaires, particulièrement la Croix-Rouge malienne, tout en décrivant une aide encore insuffisante. Elles évoquent de nombreuses femmes et des enfants parmi les déplacés, ainsi que des arrivées récentes. Certaines familles sont installées depuis quelque temps, d’autres viennent de rejoindre les localités d’accueil. Selon les deux femmes, les possibilités de reprendre une activité restent limitées. L’alerte publiée par MSF le 20 octobre, actualisée le lendemain, décrit l’urgence à Macina. Après les attaques contre Souleye le 1 er septembre et Touara le 15, plus de 3 400 personnes ont rejoint une ville qui accueillait déjà plus de 5 000 déplacés. L’organisation signale le retrait de plusieurs acteurs internationaux de cette zone, faute de financements. La majorité des déplacés sont hébergés par des familles d’accueil, tandis que d’autres vivent dans la rue, rapporte MSF. Ces ménages doivent partager des ressources déjà limitées. L’accès à l’eau, les latrines et les abris figurent parmi les besoins signalés par l’organisation. Pour les arrivées enregistrées du 30 juillet au 16 septembre, Modibo Diarra, Coordinateur du projet humanitaire d’ALPHALOG, fait état de 475 ménages, soit 2 586 personnes, recensés par les services sociaux. Parmi elles figurent 439 enfants de moins de 5 ans. Ces familles, venues de Mérou-Daga, Souleye, Kèllè et Touara, se sont installées dans la ville de Macina. Financement largement déficitaire À l’échelle nationale, le Plan des besoins et de la réponse humanitaire 2026 cible 3,8 millions de personnes sur 5,1 millions ayant besoin d’assistance. Selon les données OCHA citées par AMSODE, le plan nécessitait l’équivalent d’environ 338,7 milliards de francs CFA. Au 28 septembre, 79,5 milliards avaient été mobilisés, soit 23,5%. Il restait donc 259,2 milliards à trouver. Les conséquences sont déjà décrites par le Programme alimentaire mondial. Dans sa réponse d’urgence, le PAM indique que les contraintes financières l’ont empêché d’assister plus de 200 000 personnes vulnérables en 2026. La durée de l’aide a également été ramenée de 6 à 3 mois. Le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies pour les réfugiés (HCR) signalait pour sa propre opération au Mali un financement de 22% au 30 septembre, dans son bilan publié le 20 octobre. ALPHALOG a vécu une interruption suivie d’une reprise. Selon Modibo Diarra, l’arrêt des financements de l’USAID a entraîné la suspension du projet le 25 janvier 2025. Les distributions et les activités de protection ont été interrompues. Les interventions ont repris le 1 er avril grâce à un financement du gouvernement américain passant par son ambassade à Bamako. Dans le cadre de son partenariat avec CECI Mali, dont la dernière période d’intervention s’est achevée le 31 mars 2026, l’ONG a réalisé d’autres distributions. À Macina, 558 ménages ont notamment reçu en janvier des rations couvrant 3 mois. Des kits de cuisine ont été distribués en février dans les communes de Macina et de Kokry. Accès difficile Les difficultés d’accès renchérissent aussi les interventions. ALPHALOG décrit les obstacles rencontrés pour atteindre les villages situés hors de Macina. Des activités ont été déplacées vers la ville et des distributions organisées dans les chefs-lieux de commune jugés plus sûrs. Faire venir les bénéficiaires occasionne des coûts supplémentaires, initialement absents du budget. Pour maintenir le lien, l’organisation utilise des radios partenaires et des jeunes points focaux formés dans les villages difficiles d’accès. Les déplacements des équipes suivent un protocole de sécurité. Un nouveau projet multisectoriel pour 2026 - 2027 doit soutenir les déplacés et les communautés d’accueil de Macina. Financé par le Fonds humanitaire régional pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre, géré par OCHA, il a déjà donné lieu au versement d’une première avance de 40%, précise Modibo Diarra. Les préparatifs sont achevés. L’organisation dit attendre l’avis de non-objection de l’Administration territoriale pour démarrer. Soins médicaux cruciaux À Macina, AMSODE intervient avec une équipe mobile intégrée. Dr Traoré Aminata Simpara, Coordinatrice Santé et Nutrition, explique que ce dispositif rapproche les services des populations, pour lesquelles l’accès aux structures de soins est difficile. La clinique mobile de MSF a de son côté pris en charge 2 131 personnes du 23 septembre au 7 octobre. Les équipes décrivent notamment des infections respiratoires et des cas de paludisme, dans un environnement marqué par le manque d’abris et d’équipements sanitaires. Entre février et septembre 2026, une intervention d’AMSODE a permis d’assurer 13 269 consultations curatives gratuites dans 7 régions, de Tombouctou à Ségou. Elle a également appuyé 272 urgences obstétricales et néonatales et dépisté 1 545 enfants pour la malnutrition. L’appui financier peut aussi permettre un suivi médical auparavant inaccessible. Dans un témoignage transmis par AMSODE, Boura Guindo explique avoir reçu 105 000 francs CFA pour accompagner sa grossesse. Cette somme lui a permis de réaliser 3 échographies et d’autres analyses. « Sans cette somme, je n’aurais pas pu assurer correctement le suivi de ma grossesse », témoigne-t-elle. Alimatou Karembé, dont le témoignage a également été transmis par l’organisation, a reçu le même montant. Elle explique avoir réalisé 3 échographies pendant sa dernière grossesse, alors qu’elle n’avait jamais pu bénéficier d’un suivi médical lors des précédentes. La Coordinatrice rappelle toutefois qu’« une assistance peut également prendre fin alors que les ménages concernés n’ont pas encore retrouvé leur autonomie ». Elle insiste aussi sur les familles d’accueil, qui partagent leurs ressources et peuvent elles-mêmes vivre dans la précarité. Mobilisation tous azimuts La Croix-Rouge malienne indique assister actuellement plus de 300 ménages déplacés dans les zones de Macina et de l’interfleuve entre Mopti et Ségou. Originaires notamment de Macina et de Niono, ils reçoivent des kits d’hygiène et d’assainissement, des kits de dignité et des moustiquaires. Les interventions s’étendent à d’autres foyers de déplacement. À Ménaka, 600 ménages ont récemment reçu une assistance financière. À Diré, dans la région de Tombouctou, 2 000 ménages ont bénéficié de transferts de 50 000 francs CFA chacun, pour une enveloppe totale de 100 millions. Nouhoum Maïga, Directeur général de la Croix-Rouge malienne, annonce plus de 10 milliards de francs CFA mobilisés sur des besoins estimés à 12 milliards pour 2026. Parmi les appuis cités figure une contribution américaine de 3 millions de dollars au troisième trimestre, soit environ 1,8 milliard de francs CFA. Les démarches de mobilisation se poursuivent auprès de partenaires en Europe et dans les pays arabes. Avec plus de 10 200 volontaires, l’organisation s’appuie sur ses branches et ses unités locales pour maintenir sa présence. Son Directeur plaide pour des financements prévisibles et souples, adaptés à l’évolution des besoins, ainsi que pour un soutien accru aux acteurs nationaux présents auprès des communautés. Pour AMSODE, l’accompagnement doit aussi couvrir la protection et le soutien psychosocial. Les pertes de biens et de revenus, les séparations familiales et les difficultés d’accès à l’école prolongent les conséquences du déplacement. La Coordinatrice demande de soutenir les familles d’accueil autant que les nouveaux arrivants. Le soutien aux moyens d’existence figure également parmi les demandes d’AMSODE. À Ségou, les deux déplacées rencontrées évoquent l’appui à la scolarisation et les petites activités que certaines femmes tentent de développer grâce aux organisations. Elles saluent ces soutiens. Mais, pour leur quotidien, elles citent toujours les mêmes priorités : des vivres et des abris. Massiré Diop

items.title: Sucreries du Gabon : les ventes s’effondrent, les salariés s’inquiètent, le spectre d’une fermeture plane
items.description: Confrontées à des difficultés d’écoulement de leur production, les Sucreries du Gabon alertent sur la dégradation de leur activité. Entre janvier et septembre 2026, l’entreprise a généré 7,43 milliards de FCFA de recettes commerciales, tandis que son activité industrielle reculait de 25,3 %. Des sacs de sucre attendant des acheteurs dans l'entrepôt de la société. © GabonReview Les Sucreries du Gabon font face à une situation économique préoccupante. Près de Franceville, dans le Haut-Ogooué, les responsables de l’entreprise dénoncent la baisse des ventes de sucre, notamment auprès des industriels, dont les achats constituaient une part importante de leur chiffre d’affaires. Une difficulté qui pèse sur la production et ravive les inquiétudes autour de l’avenir de cet outil industriel. Selon les données présentées récemment par ses employés, l’entreprise a enregistré 7,43 milliards de FCFA de recettes issues de la vente de sucre entre janvier et septembre 2026, soit une moyenne mensuelle d’environ 826 millions de FCFA. Malgré ces revenus, son activité industrielle aurait reculé de 25,3 %. Les industriels au cœur des difficultés commerciales « Aujourd’hui, nous avons une difficulté particulière de pouvoir vendre le sucre parce que les industriels qui constituaient le plus gros de notre chiffre d’affaires n’achètent pas de sucre chez nous » , explique Paul Francis Mvomo, directeur des ressources humaines. Le responsable appelle l’État à prendre en considération cette situation afin de permettre à l’entreprise de retrouver une santé financière. Il s’interroge également sur l’ampleur du phénomène, qu’il juge inhabituel par rapport à la période de la Sucaf, l’ancienne dénomination de l’entreprise. L’avenir du site inquiète les salariés Rachetés en avril 2024 par l’État gabonais, les actifs de l’ancienne Sucaf sont désormais exploités sous l’appellation Sucreries du Gabon, avec le groupe turc MFB International comme actionnaire majoritaire à 90 %, contre 10 % pour l’État. Les difficultés actuelles ne sont pas nouvelles. En septembre, le gouvernement avait déjà engagé une réflexion sur les conditions de relance de l’entreprise, après une visite de l'ex-ministre de l’Industrie et de la Transformation locale, Lubin Ntoutoume. L’examen de la chaîne de production avait notamment porté sur les plantations, les installations industrielles, le transport et le conditionnement. Sur le terrain, les salariés redoutent une répétition du scénario de la Société sucrière du Haut-Ogooué (SOSUHO), autrefois fermée. « Il n’a qu’à faire le tout possible de nous trouver quand même quelqu’un qui va nous garder » , implore un employé. Au-delà des emplois, l’enjeu concerne la pérennité de la production sucrière nationale et la capacité du Gabon à préserver son tissu industriel. L’article Sucreries du Gabon : les ventes s’effondrent, les salariés s’inquiètent, le spectre d’une fermeture plane est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: He Wanted to Save Children. Instead, He Unleashed Chaos.
items.description: Editor's Note: This story is one in a three-part series commemorating the 10-year anniversary of Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory that led to a shooting at the Washington, D.C., restaurant Comet Ping Pong in 2016. Read Kaitlyn Tiffany’s analysis on the legacy of Pizzagate and Ross Andersen’s story about Comet Ping Pong . I n the video, recorded from the dashboard of his Toyota Prius, he looks at times like he’s on the verge of tears. Edgar Maddison Welch makes a point to look into the camera when he speaks. That’s because the video is for his two children. He speaks slowly; it’s unclear whether he’s weighing each word or simply unsure of what to say. Somewhere in the back of the car are the AR-15, the shotgun, and the .38-caliber revolver he’s brought with him. “I can’t let you grow up in a world that’s so corrupted by evil without at least standing up for you, and for other children,” he says. His demeanor is calm and there’s resignation in his voice. “Like I’ve always told you, we have a duty to protect people who can’t protect themselves and do for people who can’t do for themselves. That’s what I’m trying to do. I hope you understand that one day.” Back home in Salisbury, North Carolina, his girlfriend was not pleased. He’d left the children with her early that morning, while she was still asleep. He’d texted her that he loved her, and she’d responded with a barrage of angry replies; “idk what the fuck Ur doing it’s really starting to freak me out,” she’d written. “Jus know that the ppl u love R suffering too back home.” This impromptu six-hour road trip was nothing more than a “selfish lil adventure.” He did not see it that way. This was God’s work. Not long after leaving home, he’d texted a friend a verse from the Book of Isaiah: “He has sent me to comfort the brokenhearted and to proclaim that captives will be released and prisoners will be freed.” Tattooed on his back was a different verse from the same book—that “those who hope in the Lord” will be made strong in his image. “They will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not be faint.” Welch, who went by his middle name, Maddison, must have felt, in that moment, like he was living the scripture. Near the end of his journey, he texted his friends, asking them to take care of his family. Finally, around 3 p.m. on December 4, 2016, he arrived at his destination: a family pizza restaurant in an affluent neighborhood of Washington, D.C. He left his phone in the car but brought the guns. Holding an assault rifle across his chest, the 28-year-old walked through the front door of Comet Ping Pong in search of something that didn’t exist. The employees and families dining inside who saw him enter panicked and scrambled to leave. Just 24 minutes later, Welch walked out the same door, unarmed, with his hands in the air. Nobody had been hurt, but something had suddenly changed. Welch had gone to Comet Ping Pong to look for proof of a global elite-pedophile ring in the basement. He’d been watching YouTube videos from online shock jocks, who suggested that Comet was the site of untold horrors. It made him feel sick. Maybe he thought he would come across a hidden room full of shackled children, or a network of tunnels. Perhaps, as the conspiracies suggested, he’d catch the Clinton or Podesta families in some grotesque act. The scenario he hadn’t prepared himself for was the one in which he found nothing at all. After firing three shots at the lock of the storage-closet door, Welch saw that it contained no secret room, no ring, no conspiracy. The story of Welch, the Pizzagate shooter, as it is often told, is that of a man searching for a revelation that never arrived. But that’s not true. Welch experienced a genuine epiphany: It seems that, after entering, he could no longer deny the reality that Comet was, as any reasonable person could see, just a regular restaurant. Faced with the truth, he peacefully surrendered to police. Those following the news experienced a revelation, too, only the opposite: Welch represented an incursion of a dark, lawless online world of lies into our reality. Ten years ago, this reckless act felt more like a glitch of internet-addled, lone-wolf vigilantism. Over time, Welch has become a sadly familiar archetype—a poster boy for a long-running crisis that includes QAnon and January 6. In the aftermath of Welch’s arrest, the gunman famously told The New York Times , “The intel on this wasn’t 100 percent.” He didn’t know it then, but the phrase would turn out to be a solid epitaph for our paranoid and turbulent times. “W e are a family of rescuers,” Welch’s mother, Terri Welch, wrote in a statement shortly after the shooting. Those who knew the family described her and the shooter’s father, Harry Welch, to me as both religious and civic-minded. Terri had become a volunteer firefighter in her mid-50s, and Harry Sr. seems to have done it all. According to his IMDb page, in addition to being a screenwriter, Harry Sr. was an NRA firearms instructor who taught gun-safety classes to elementary-school students; a foster parent; and a former member of drug task forces. He claims he has held seven Guinness World Records, only one of which could I find any evidence of: a 1986 record for most consecutive one-armed push-ups. While Welch was growing up, Harry Sr. served as executive director of Protect-A-Child, a nonprofit organization for preventing child abuse and abduction. The family ran an animal rescue too. Christian Dionne, Welch’s childhood friend, told me that their house was a “wild place,” full of dozens of dogs, as well as exotic and taxidermied animals, including at least one tiger. Maddison—his friends sometimes called him Momo—had a magnetic personality. He was known to be easygoing and open. He was “the epitome of cool” even at a young age, Dionne said. A goofball obsessed with early-aughts shows such as Jackass and punch-you-in-the-nuts humor, he was privately nerdy. On weekend nights, Welch’s friends would hangout at Harry Sr.’s store for LAN parties, where they played Counter-Strike until the early hours. Welch was, according to Dionne, “very into weapons” and had scythes and throwing stars. From what can be gleaned from court records and those who knew him, Welch’s life after high school suggests an optimistic, though frenetic personality. He was prone to taking bold action like his parents: In the fall of 2009, he embarked on an impulsive, poorly timed hike of the difficult, 500-mile Colorado Trail. A local newspaper interviewed him about his adventure, depicting him as indefatigable, energized by braving blizzard conditions and even fending off a bear. In 2010, he flew down to Haiti for three weeks with a church group after a devastating earthquake and helped rebuild an orphanage. According to the pastor who accompanied him, he became so invested in the kids that he would “forgo eating and give his food to the children.” Welch surfed, hiked, and hung out with family, but he mostly seemed aimless. His employment history was spotty. “I had the impression he was basically kind of homeless for these periods,” Demian Ahn, the lead prosecutor in Welch’s case, told me. He was raising his two kids as a single parent. Some years later, he joined the local fire department as a volunteer firefighter and began working toward a paid role. And then, 41 days before his arrest at Comet, on the way to his job at a grocery warehouse, Welch hit a boy with his Buick LeSabre. Thirteen-year-old Kenyatta Belton was badly injured and airlifted to the hospital. Welch, who was driving the speed limit and not impaired, reportedly stayed with Belton at the scene. The accident, Welch’s parents told a reporter, changed his behavior. Belton survived, but it’s easy to imagine Welch drawing a parallel to a much earlier incident in his life—something he’d never talked about, according to a friend. In 1997, just before Welch turned 9, his brother, Harry Jr., died in a car accident. After the incident with Belton, according to The Washington Post , Welch suffered nightmares and was racked with guilt. He grew anxious and moody, and it seems like his life soon began to unravel. He was caring for his children during the day and working 12-hour shifts at night. At some point, the fire department removed Welch from its roster for being inactive. Illustration by Joan Wong. Source: Gage Skidmore / ZUMA Press Wire / Reuters. T he narrative that developed after the Pizzagate shooting was that Welch was something of a hyper-online lunatic. But compared with many of the extremists who followed, Welch had a scant online footprint. The 2009 local-news article about his hiking expedition mentions, with no other context, that the trip had “broken his addiction to the Internet.” Still, Welch had little more than a Facebook page. The Daily Beast reported that he’d “liked” a Facebook page for Alex Jones’s former conspiracy site, Infowars. Welch later told The New York Times that he thought Jones “touches on some issues that are viable but goes off the deep end.” Ahn, who had access to Welch’s internet history, told me that he saw a high volume of online activity in the lead-up to the shooting, especially on Facebook Messenger. “His brain was moving so fast to try and connect dots to make sense of things and with a very undisciplined religiosity,” he said. Available court records, which include data collected from Welch’s phone, show one multihour online binge on the evening of December 1, 2016—mostly YouTube, Messenger, and lots of texting. Welch told reporters that he’d first heard of Pizzagate through word of mouth. The conspiracy theory had surfaced online just before the 2016 presidential election; trolls and vigilante Reddit investigators had seized on leaked emails from Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and were suggesting that Washington elites had organized an elaborate child-trafficking ring that ran through places such as Comet Ping Pong. In court evidence, you can see that Welch had sent friends links to feverish videos about Pizzagate that have since been taken down. In one, Jones tells his audience, “You have to go investigate it for yourself.” Another Infowars video explicitly references Comet Ping Pong and ends by calling out its owner, James Alefantis: “Either you are the unlucky victim of a fake-news onslaught [due to your own poorly initiated publicity] or a decades-old pedophile ring operating in the power-hoarding shadows of Washington, D.C., is about to be opened from your front door.” Four days after sending the video, Welch walked through that front door. Three months later, he pleaded guilty to interstate transportation of firearms and ammunition, and assault with a dangerous weapon. At his trial, his friends and family spoke to his character, spirituality, and devoted parenting. Comet Ping Pong employees delivered emotional testimony about their post-traumatic stress and how Welch had shaken their community with violence. Some offered their empathy to Welch, who apologized at his sentencing but did not explicitly renounce Pizzagate. Welch was sentenced to 48 months in prison. And, on May 28, 2020, he was released into the early months of the pandemic. His life, or what can be gleaned from it through social media and news reports, seemed to follow two paths at once. The first shows a man embracing his second chance: Welch got a job at a restaurant and reunited with his girlfriend—the one he’d left with the kids. The pair had two children together after his release. Welch appears to have made a new Facebook account, using the name “Eddie Wood.” Photos on his and his girlfriend’s profiles show Welch quite active: hiking with his family, smiling with his parents at a Christmas carnival, attending a comics convention. He appears consistently happy—always making funny faces for the camera. Scrolling through the idyllic posts, I was reminded of a quote he’d given to his hometown paper in 2009: “I can’t imagine what the rest of the world offers.” Welch’s second path is documented via police blotters and obituaries. In February 2024, Welch and his girlfriend were arrested early one morning. Welch was booked after a cop found heroin and drug paraphernalia in his car; his girlfriend received extra charges for hiding meth on her during their jail booking. In his mug shot, Welch appears disheveled, his eyes nearly closed. On Christmas Day 2024, Welch was booked by Kannapolis, North Carolina, police for a failure to appear in court for possession of drug paraphernalia. And then, on January 4, 2025, police stopped a vehicle that Welch was riding in. The officer—the same one who had arrested him a few days earlier—recognized Welch and approached his door. Welch pulled out a handgun and pointed it at the officer. Officers told him to drop the weapon. He did not. The officers opened fire. Welch was taken to the hospital, where he died from gunshot wounds on January 6. W hat is somebody supposed to do with the entirety of Welch’s awful story? It’s possible to see Welch as little more than a selfish bully. Or a sad sack, a once-popular kid who peaked in high school, who didn’t get out and then watched his life fall apart. Maybe he was a dupe who immediately realized he was wrong after going too far. A devoted dad led astray by the lies of others, or a religious nut who abandoned his girlfriend and children after watching some YouTube videos. Ten years on, as I’ve pored over the contents of his ruined life and spoken with the few people who were willing to relive the story with a reporter, all that’s clear is how little Welch, the man, means to Pizzagate. When he failed to give conspiracy theorists the evidence they craved that day, they dubbed him a crisis actor. He was neither memorialized nor remembered, other than as a harbinger of the darkness that might follow in the then-new Trump era. The only thing that made him newsworthy at all was the potential violence he’d been prepared to carry out. His legacy may be best captured by a portion of the original URL of the Daily Beast ’s story about the shooting: fake-news-delivers-real-gunman . What exactly did the Pizzagate movement mean to Welch? Ahn, the prosecutor, told me he believed that Welch’s fears and anger around Pizzagate were genuine. Unlike a lot of other modern shooters, who seem to be performing for an online audience, he didn’t film his attack, and it doesn’t appear that he did it for clout. Nor does it seem like Welch made any attempts to capitalize on his infamy with the Pizzagate crowd. He seems to have been a true believer. And yet, there is no record that he continued with the cause after prison. When he got out, he went back to his life in Salisbury. For the rest of society, Welch primarily functioned as a model for the rise of a type of guy who, faced with his own unmooring, finds momentary purpose in a durable, networked fantasy. “If you don’t have a whole lot going on in your life, we’ve seen people can get so wrapped up in these narratives that they start acting as if they’re real,” Logan Strain, a co-host of the QAnon Anonymous podcast, told me. “It becomes this participatory soap opera.” Two years after Welch entered Comet Ping Pong, Matthew Wright barricaded a bridge to the Hoover Dam with an armored vehicle, holding a sign that read Release the OIG report, referring to a set of documents that QAnon believers thought would expose Democrats engaging in criminal and conspiratorial behavior. Then there was Cesar Sayoc—a man who sent 16 pipe bombs to CNN, as well as Barack Obama, Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, and other politicians critical of Donald Trump. His van, discovered at the time of his arrest, was covered in 4chan-style memes. The Tree of Life shooter, Robert Bowers, was posting on the alt-right social network Gab up until opening fire in the synagogue. David DePape, who had been obsessed with Pizzagate and QAnon content, broke into the home of Nancy Pelosi and assaulted her husband with a hammer. These men left behind digital breadcrumbs that would become the hallmarks of a modern extremist—mounting evidence of people becoming more and more angry, frantic, and erratic until they finally take matters into their own hands. Some observers trace a straight line from Welch to the individuals who, fueled by a false belief that the 2020 election had been stolen, stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021. “It’s all people reaching the climax of the fever dream,” Strain said. “And it starts to unravel as they cross the threshold.” When that happens, some, like Welch, lay down their weapons; others turn to unspeakable violence. The underlying dynamics behind the YouTube-to-gunman pipeline are nothing new. In his famous 1964 essay, “The Paranoid Style in American Politics,” Richard Hofstadter wrote, “We are all sufferers from history, but the paranoid is a double sufferer, since he is afflicted not only by the real world, with the rest of us, but by his fantasies as well.” The difference now is that our technology compounds and democratizes that suffering via an algorithmic feedback loop of fantasies that grow only more angry and deranged. Today, we can all be sufferers of history twice over: once by real-world violence, and again by the imagined world that the paranoid force us to attend to. Moments before Welch was sentenced, a Comet Ping Pong employee addressed the defendant directly. “I’m almost sorry you were duped,” the employee said. “That you fell into the trap of an orchestrated game created by hateful people whose intention it is to create fear and mistrust amongst the public. I’m almost sorry that the same people that inspired you to travel from North Carolina and come to my place of work with an assault rifle now believe you’re a hired actor. That’s how misinformation works and the game is played.” There’s grace in those words. They also illustrate the cycle of suffering bestowed on those who choose to submit to lies. Pizzagate didn’t end when Welch found nothing. To the conspiracy machine he briefly served, he was ultimately little more than a useful idiot, grist for the mill. His death eight years later made only brief headlines, overshadowed by the anniversary of the Capitol riots and a forthcoming Trump inauguration. Many of those who had trafficked the lies that led Welch to Comet Ping Pong didn’t even note his passing. Welch’s is a particularly American tragedy. “Maddison was always, especially after his brother died, looking for something to believe in,” Dionne, his childhood friend, told me. And so Edgar Maddison Welch entered a pizza parlor hoping to find a monster. Turns out, it was him.

items.title: The Epstein-Pizzagate Connection
items.description: Editor's Note: This story is one in a three-part series commemorating the 10-year anniversary of Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory that led to a shooting at the Washington, D.C., restaurant Comet Ping Pong in 2016. Read Ross Andersen’s story about Comet Ping Pong and Charlie Warzel’s profile of the Pizzagate shooter , Edgar Maddison Welch. This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. E arlier this year, on his very popular podcast, Tucker Carlson brought up a “semi-forgotten story” that he had once found absurd. “I didn’t take Pizzagate as seriously, maybe, as I guess I should have at the time,” he said. The time he was referring to is the late fall of 2016, just before and after the first election of Donald Trump, when the details of an imagined pedophilia ring that was organized by powerful Democrats began to spread online. The Pizzagate conspiracy theory was drawn from a batch of hacked emails from Hillary Clinton’s campaign chairman, John Podesta, who had corresponded with the owner of a Washington, D.C., pizza restaurant called Comet Ping Pong. Podesta had sent a bunch of emails about pizza. It’s not worth your time for me to explain why some people became convinced that these were full of coded references to child sex slaves. The important thing to know or remember is that, by early December, the theory was spilling over into practice. Edgar Welch, a 28-year-old North Carolina man, arrived at Comet one Sunday afternoon with a revolver and an AR-15, under the assumption that he would find and free the children being kept there. Now everyone could see that the aspersion-casting had gone too far. One of the leading Pizzagate influencers, Alex Jones, publicly apologized to Comet’s owner, presumably to avoid a lawsuit , and one of Trump’s favored far-right influencers, Jack Posobiec—a guy who had once barged into the restaurant himself, with a camera rolling—backed off too, eventually insisting that he had never even claimed the conspiracy was real. Pizzagate had become embarrassing, even to its early promoters. But any trace of shame is now a distant memory. Ten years after its inception, Carlson is interested in Pizzagate—and regretful that he wasn’t interested before. In this, he’s not alone. Last January, when the government released millions of pages of files related to the crimes of Jeffrey Epstein, one subset of internet sleuths began by searching them for mentions of “pizza.” They found many. On his podcast, Carlson said he was intrigued by several in which Epstein and his urologist discussed going out for “pizza and grape soda,” a combination that Carlson found so absurd as to be suspicious. “Maybe this is code,” he said. Carlson’s guest, an up-and-coming conspiracy-theory YouTuber named Ian Carroll, encouraged him to keep thinking. What if Welch’s storming of the pizzeria was not, after all, a sad example of the internet’s power to mislead, but rather something else: a cover-up? Sure, Welch had burst into Comet and terrorized the customers and employees within, but not a single person had been physically harmed (convenient). Welch’s bullets did end up damaging a computer (convenient), which may have contained who knows what kind of information (convenient). After Welch was arrested, he gave (convenient) quotes to reporters about how he’d been misled by online sources. That neat story, Carroll implied, had been designed to make it seem like any question-asking along the lines of Pizzagate was dangerous and wrong. Carlson seemed convinced. When the interview went up on YouTube (where it currently has 2.7 million views), the video description read, “It looks like Pizzagate is basically real.” The same conclusion has in recent years been percolating throughout mainstream social-media platforms, where moderation rules once restricted discussion of Pizzagate. Following the Welch incident, nearly all of them made some effort to block Pizzagate-related hashtags or at least add warning labels to Pizzagate-related content—but these measures are no longer in place. “It’s become en vogue to revisit this theory,” Samuel Woolley, an associate professor and chair in disinformation studies at the University of Pittsburgh, told me. Back in 2016, Pizzagate was interpreted as a close call and taken as a warning. It was a sign that any of the turbid fantasies that swirl around in online spaces might lap across the boundary with real life. But the shocking power of that revelation—drawn from an episode in which nobody got hurt and the shooter apologized—is hard to fathom now. More thorough bendings of reality have long since become the norm, and the barrier between the online and offline worlds is all but gone. W hen government prosecutors asked that Edgar Welch be given 54 months in prison for his pizza-joint invasion, they cited the need to “deter other would-be vigilantes from attempting similar crimes against innocent subjects of the next internet-inspired conspiracy theory.” They said they thought it was important to make sure that such a weird thing never happened again. Demian Ahn, who served as one of those prosecutors, told me that the sum total of all of the evidence in the case—what was on Welch’s phone, what his friends and family had said in interviews—indicated that Welch’s motivations were sincere. He really thought that he was going to be saving children from the basement of a pizza place. “He seemed to be a well-meaning person,” Ahn said. “He believed that Washington, D.C., as a city, was so corrupt that you could have a child-exploitation ring openly operated by prominent people at a regular restaurant.” How exactly Welch had come to this belief would be the subject of various postmortems in the years that followed. These did not agree on where and how the Pizzagate story gained its crucial momentum: Some experts said that anonymous posters on 4chan drove the theory’s spread; others claimed that ordinary Facebook users played the most important role. Russian propagandists certainly were involved, eagerly reposting #Pizzagate content, but so were right-wing influencers in the United States. However it emerged, Pizzagate did fade for a while after Welch’s arrest, before returning in expanded form with QAnon . That sprawling belief system took hold near the end of Trump’s first term, and imagined the president as an avenging angel, bringing violent justice to a network of Satanic Democrats who were after children’s blood. When social platforms cracked down on QAnon in 2020 and 2021, on account of its connection to the storming of the Capitol, the Pizzagate theory got tamped down once again. But it never really went away. Trump campaigned for his second term in part by incorporating QAnon slogans and themes into his messaging. Today’s Pizzagate believers take a broader view than Welch did. As Samuel Woolley put it, they may not claim that all of the details of the theory were right on target—that there really was a basement full of trafficked children in a pizza place in D.C.—“but that the general thrust of the argument was correct.” (When Carlson and Carroll riffed on the theory, this is how they talked.) Many people now assert that Epstein started Pizzagate himself, to draw attention away from his own child-sex-related crimes, Woolley told me. They point suggestively to evidence that Epstein once met with 4chan’s founder . Carlson, too, seems preoccupied with Epstein’s connection to Pizzagate. I reached out to him this fall, and when we spoke by phone, he kept returning to the same text-message exchange that he’d cited on his podcast, between Epstein and the billionaire’s urologist. “No rich white person drinks grape soda, period,” Carlson said. “Grape soda is probably more unfashionable than cigarettes among rich people. I just want to say that unequivocally. Where do you even buy grape soda?” Any reference to it in the texts was obviously code for something , he insisted. He just didn’t know for what. T oday’s conspiracy theories are ornate. They animate online communities of all different political bents and cultural referents, and they overlap in surprising and strange ways. Take Ian Carroll, the guest on Carlson’s podcast, who is better known for filling in as the host of Candace Owens’s show while she was on maternity leave. He has launched an interactive tool called the “Webb,” which allows evidence from disparate public sources to be pieced together. Anyone can use his string-board engine to connect documents from the Epstein files to those concerning, among other things, UFOs, 9/11, the Zodiac Killer, and the murder of Charlie Kirk. (Carroll did not respond to requests for an interview.) A site like that may still be somewhat of a niche concern, but a paranoid attitude has clearly become more widespread in our culture since 2016. An attempted assassination at the White House Correspondent’s Dinner, a flood in Texas , or a football team’s failure —none are necessarily accepted as what they seem. The facts themselves may not always matter so much as the thrill of riffing and guessing. At one point in the Pizzagate episode of his podcast, Carlson told Carroll that he thought he’d heard that the shooter ended up getting killed right before the Epstein files came out. “Is that true?” he asked. “I heard the same reporting,” Carroll said. “Obviously, at this point, I don’t really know what’s true. The whole world feels a little bit like The Matrix .” In fact, the timeline is unambiguous: Edgar Welch was shot and killed by police in January 2025 after pointing a gun at an officer during a traffic stop; the Epstein files were released in December of that year. Later, when I spoke with Carlson on the phone, he explained that he’d disregarded Pizzagate originally because he’d been too close to it. Literally, he’d lived near Comet and taken his children there for pizza. He knew John Podesta, his brother, and his brother’s wife personally, and he knew the pizza-shop owner too. “It seemed so far-out, I don’t think I spent 10 minutes thinking about it.” Now he lives in Maine and eats gas-station pizza, he told me. And he is very confused as to why the Epstein files’ references to pizza and grape soda haven’t gotten more attention from media and law enforcement. “Everyone is effectively covering for Epstein—why?” he said. “I don’t know the answer.” After we hung up, I reasoned that it was fair to ask a journalist to look into this matter, so I did. Epstein and his urologist talked about pizza and grape soda at least five times in 2018, the year before Epstein’s death. I couldn’t reach the urologist by phone to ask why. But on one occasion , he’d accompanied his text with a photo. He was in a pizza shop, having a cheese slice with a bottle of Crush grape soda. *Illustration source: Mugshot Zone
